quiz.explain: A quick read of the whole paper helps you choose an order, spot instructions and plan your time before you commit.

quiz.q: How should you divide your time across questions?
options: As much time as you want on the first question
In line with how many marks each question carries
Spend most time on the questions you know best
quiz.explain: Matching time to marks stops you spending twenty minutes on a two-mark question and rushing the big ones.

quiz.q: Why plan a long answer before writing it?
options: Examiners give marks for the plan alone
It keeps the answer focused and organised
It is only useful if you have extra time
quiz.explain: One minute of planning helps you include the key points in a clear order, which is what earns marks in long answers.

lessons.title: Calm under exam pressure
lessons.content:
Some nervousness before an exam is normal and even useful. The racing heart and alert mind are your body getting ready to perform. Instead of telling yourself to calm down, try telling yourself I am excited and ready. Treating the feeling as energy works better than fighting it.

The best cure for exam anxiety is preparation you trust. If you have planned, practised past papers and slept well, you have real evidence that you are ready. On the morning itself, keep a simple routine: a proper breakfast, everything packed the night before, and arriving early without last-minute cramming.

If your mind goes blank, do not panic. Put your pen down and breathe slowly: in for four counts, out for six, a few times. Then move to another question, or write down anything you remember about the topic. Memory often comes back once you stop forcing it and start writing.
key_points: Nerves are energy; reframe them as readiness.
Trusted preparation and a calm routine reduce anxiety.
When blank: breathe slowly, move on, write what you know.
lessons.tip: Practise slow breathing during your timed past papers too. A skill you have used under practice pressure is easier to use on the real day.
lessons.task: Write your own short exam-morning routine in five steps or fewer, and a three-step plan for what you will do if your mind goes blank. Keep it in your pencil case.

quiz.q: What is a helpful way to think about exam nerves?
options: As a sign that you will fail
As something you must hide from everyone
As proof that you did not study enough
As energy that helps your body get ready
quiz.explain: Reframing nerves as excitement and readiness turns the same body signals into something that helps you perform.

quiz.q: What reduces exam anxiety the most?
options: Studying all night before the exam
Preparation you trust and a simple exam-morning routine
Avoiding all thoughts about the exam
Comparing answers with friends just before going in
quiz.explain: Real preparation gives you evidence that you are ready, and a calm routine removes avoidable stress on the day.

quiz.q: Your mind goes blank on a question. What should you do first?
options: Keep staring at the question until it comes back
Breathe slowly, then move on or write what you remember
Guess randomly and stop thinking about it
quiz.explain: Slow breathing calms the stress response, and moving on or writing related points often brings the memory back.

lessons.title: Learn anything new quickly
lessons.content:
The physicist Richard Feynman had a simple test for understanding: if you cannot explain something in plain words, you do not really know it yet. The Feynman technique turns that test into a study method you can use on any subject.

It has four steps. Pick a topic and write its name at the top of a page. Explain it in simple words, as if teaching a younger student, without copying from the book. Wherever you get stuck, use jargon you cannot explain or skip a step, you have found a gap. Go back to the source, fill that gap, and explain it again.

The power of the method is that it shows you exactly what you do not know. Rereading hides gaps behind familiar words, while explaining exposes them. Each round makes your explanation shorter and clearer, and a clear explanation is a sign the idea is truly yours.
key_points: If you cannot explain it simply, you do not fully understand it yet.
Explain the topic in plain words as if to a younger student.
The places where you get stuck show you exactly what to study next.
lessons.tip: Ban yourself from using any technical word you could not define on the spot. If you need it, explain it first in everyday language.
lessons.task: Choose one hard concept from your current subject and explain it in plain words in under 100 words, without looking at your notes. Underline every place where you got stuck, then check the book and rewrite those parts.

quiz.q: What is the main idea behind the Feynman technique?
options: Read the chapter as many times as possible
Memorise the exact definitions from the textbook
Explain a topic simply to find the gaps in your understanding
Study only with a teacher present
quiz.explain: Explaining in plain words reveals what you do not yet understand, so you know exactly where to go back and study.

quiz.q: While explaining a topic, you keep using a term you cannot define. What should you do?
options: Treat it as a gap, look it up and explain it in simple words
Ignore it, because the examiner will know what it means
Replace it with a longer technical word
Move on to a different topic
quiz.explain: Jargon you cannot explain is a sign of a gap. Filling it is the whole point of the technique.

quiz.q: Why does explaining work better than rereading for finding what you do not know?
options: Explaining takes less time than reading
Rereading makes words feel familiar, while explaining forces you to produce the idea yourself
Rereading is only useful for maths
Explaining lets you skip the hard parts
quiz.explain: Familiar words create an illusion of knowing. Producing the explanation yourself shows clearly what is missing.

lessons.title: Study with others
lessons.content:
Studying with others can make learning faster and more enjoyable. When you explain a topic to a friend, you organise it in your own head, and when a friend asks you a question you had not thought of, you discover a new gap. Teaching is one of the strongest ways to learn.

Good study groups use active methods. Members take turns teaching a small part, quiz each other with questions written in advance and compare answers to past problems. Hearing how someone else solved a problem shows you a different way of thinking about it.

The risk is that a group turns into chatting. Keep it small, three to five people, and agree on a clear goal before you meet, such as finishing one chapter's questions. Give each person a role, set a time limit, and end with a short quiz so everyone leaves knowing what they actually learned.
key_points: Teaching a friend is one of the best ways to learn.
Use the group for active work: teaching, quizzing and solving problems.
A clear goal, roles and a time limit stop the group from becoming chatting.
lessons.tip: Do your own study first and come to the group with questions. A group is best for testing and explaining, not for reading the book together for the first time.
lessons.task: Plan one group study session: write its goal, the topic each person will teach, the time limit and five quiz questions for the end. Send the plan to two or three classmates.

quiz.q: Why does teaching a topic to a friend help you learn it?
options: It lets you avoid studying on your own
Your friend will do your homework
You must organise the ideas clearly and you discover your own gaps
quiz.explain: To explain something, you have to structure it in your mind, and your friend's questions reveal what you have not understood yet.

quiz.q: Which is the best way to keep a study group focused?
options: Invite as many people as possible
Meet without a plan and see what happens
Agree on a clear goal, give each person a role and set a time limit
Only meet the night before the exam
quiz.explain: A clear goal, roles and a time limit give the session structure, so the time goes to learning rather than chatting.

quiz.q: What is a good way to end a group session?
options: A short quiz so everyone checks what they learned
quiz.explain: A closing quiz is retrieval practice. It shows each person what stuck and what still needs work.

lessons.title: Stay motivated as a student
lessons.content:
Many students wait to feel motivated before they start studying. But motivation usually comes after action, not before it. Once you start, even for five minutes, the task feels less heavy and the wish to continue grows. So the first step is to make starting very easy.

Motivation lasts longer when study is linked to something you care about. Ask yourself why a subject matters to you: a career you want, a skill you will use or simply the pride of doing well. Then track small wins, such as sessions completed or questions answered correctly. Seeing progress on paper gives you a reason to keep going.

Everyone has bad weeks. Missing a few days does not make you a failure, but guilt can turn a short break into a long one. Instead of blaming yourself, restart small: one short session today, then build back up. What matters is not a perfect record but returning quickly.
key_points: Motivation often follows action, so make starting easy.
Link each subject to your own reasons and track small wins.
After a bad week, restart small without guilt.
lessons.tip: Use the five-minute rule: promise yourself only five minutes of study. Most of the time you will keep going, and if not, you still kept the habit alive.
lessons.task: Write two or three sentences on why one subject matters to you personally. Then make a small tracker and mark three study sessions you complete this week.

quiz.q: According to this lesson, how are motivation and action usually related?
options: You must feel motivated before you can start
Motivation often comes after you start acting
They are not related at all
quiz.explain: Starting, even briefly, makes the task feel lighter and builds the wish to continue. Waiting for motivation often means never starting.

quiz.q: Which helps keep motivation over a long term?
options: Comparing yourself with the top student every day
Studying only when you feel like it
Promising yourself a huge reward at the end of the year
Linking study to your own goals and tracking small wins
quiz.explain: Personal reasons give study meaning, and visible progress gives you a reason to continue.

quiz.q: You missed a whole week of study. What is the best response?
options: Restart with one short session today and build back up
Wait until next month to start fresh
Study all night to make up for everything at once
quiz.explain: A small restart is easy to do and gets the habit going again. Guilt and all-night catch-ups usually make things worse.

lessons.title: Your personal study system
lessons.content:
You have learned many methods: active recall, spaced repetition, flashcards, Cornell notes, SQ3R, timed practice and more. Knowing them is not enough. They only work when they become a routine you follow every week, not something you try once before an exam.

A personal study system answers four questions. How will you take notes in class? How will you test yourself on them? When will you review, and at what gaps? How will you plan your week and your exams? Choose one method for each question, write them on a single page and turn them into a weekly routine with fixed days and times.

Keep the system simple enough to follow for a full term. Start with what you can keep, not with the perfect plan. After two weeks, review it: what worked, what you skipped and why. Adjust one thing at a time. A simple system you use every week beats a perfect one you abandon.
key_points: Methods only help when they become a weekly routine.
Choose one method each for notes, recall, review and planning.
Keep it simple, then review and adjust after two weeks.
lessons.tip: Attach your study blocks to things you already do every day, such as right after dinner or the first hour after school. Fixed times remove the daily decision.
lessons.task: Write your one-page study system: your note method, your self-testing method, your review schedule and your weekly plan with days and times. Put a reminder in your calendar to review it in two weeks.

quiz.q: Why build a personal study system instead of just knowing many methods?
options: So you can use a different method every day
Because methods only work when they become a regular routine
quiz.explain: Knowledge of methods does nothing on its own. A routine makes you actually use them week after week.

quiz.q: Which questions should a study system answer?
options: Who in your class studies the most
How many hours your friends study
How you take notes, test yourself, review and plan
quiz.explain: Notes, recall, spaced review and planning are the core parts. One chosen method for each makes a complete system.

quiz.q: After two weeks you notice you keep skipping one part of your system. What should you do?
options: Find out why and adjust that one part to something you can keep
Throw the whole system away and start over
Add three more methods to make up for it
Ignore it and hope it gets better
quiz.explain: Reviewing and changing one thing at a time keeps the system realistic. A simple system you follow beats a perfect one you abandon.

categories.name: Creativity
categories.tagline: Find more ideas, beat creative block and make things people want to see.
categories.description: Creativity is a skill you can practise, not a gift you either have or lack. These lessons cover generating ideas, getting unstuck, seeing like a photographer, telling stories, sharing your work and building a steady creative practice.

messages.welcome: You are more creative than you think. We will start small: one idea, one sketch, one photo at a time.
messages.comeback: Welcome back. No masterpiece needed today. Make one small, messy thing and the rest will follow.
messages.pass: Nicely done. You are starting to see the world like a maker.
messages.fail: First drafts are supposed to be rough. Read the explanations, look at the lesson again and give it another try.
messages.finished: You can now generate ideas on demand, push through creative block, compose a strong photo, shape a story, share your work and keep a practice going. Pick one small project and finish it this week.

lessons.title: Creativity is a skill, not a talent
lessons.content:
Many people say "I am just not creative", as if creativity were something you are born with or without. In reality, creativity is mostly about combining things that already exist in new ways. A new recipe mixes familiar ingredients, and a new song reuses notes everyone already knows.

Because it is about combining, creativity grows with practice and input. The more you notice, try and make, the more pieces you have to connect. People who seem naturally creative usually just have more practice and give themselves permission to try odd ideas.

So instead of asking "Am I creative?", ask "How can I practise?" Small daily habits, like looking at ordinary objects and asking what else they could be, train the same muscle that artists, designers and inventors use every day.
key_points: Creativity means combining existing ideas in new ways.
It grows with practice and varied input, not with luck at birth.
Ask how you can practise, not whether you are creative.
lessons.tip: When you catch yourself thinking "I am not creative", replace it with "I have not practised this yet". The second sentence leaves room to grow.
lessons.task: Look around and list 5 everyday things near you, like a bucket, a spoon or an old newspaper. For each one, write down one new use it was never designed for.

quiz.q: According to this lesson, what is creativity mostly about?
options: Being born with a special gift
Combining existing ideas in new ways
quiz.explain: Most new ideas are fresh combinations of things that already exist, which is why anyone can learn to make them.

quiz.q: Why do some people seem naturally creative?
options: They usually have more practice and let themselves try odd ideas
quiz.explain: What looks like talent is usually the result of many small attempts and a willingness to try strange ideas.

quiz.q: Which question helps you grow your creativity?
options: Who is more creative than me?
Why can't I be like an artist?
quiz.explain: Asking how to practise turns creativity into an action you can take, instead of a fixed label you either have or lack.

lessons.title: Quantity first, quality later
lessons.content:
Your first few ideas are usually the obvious ones, the same ideas everyone else would have. Better, more surprising ideas tend to appear only after you have pushed past those. That is why creative people aim for many ideas first and worry about good ideas later.

The trap is judging each idea the moment it appears. When you criticise while generating, your brain gets cautious and stops offering anything unusual. Treat idea-making and idea-picking as two separate steps: first collect without judging, then step back and choose.

Set a number and a time limit, like 20 ideas in 10 minutes. Silly, impractical and half-formed ideas all count. When the list is done, take a short break, then circle the two or three most promising ones and build on those.
key_points: Your first ideas are usually the most obvious ones.
Generate first, judge later, as two separate steps.
A target number and a time limit push you past the obvious.
lessons.tip: When you get stuck in the middle of a list, write a deliberately silly idea. It often unlocks a useful one right after it.
lessons.task: Pick one simple prompt, like "ways to make a rainy day fun". Set a timer for 10 minutes and write 20 ideas without crossing any out. Then circle your favourite three.

quiz.q: Why aim for many ideas before choosing one?
options: Because a long list looks impressive
Because better ideas often appear after the obvious ones
Because every idea on the list will be used
Because judging ideas is never useful
quiz.explain: The first ideas are the common ones. Pushing for quantity gets you past them to more original options.

quiz.q: What happens when you judge each idea as it appears?
options: Your brain gets cautious and stops offering unusual ideas
quiz.explain: Criticism during generation makes you play safe. Keep making and choosing as separate steps.

quiz.q: During the 20-ideas exercise, what should you do with a silly idea?
options: Write it down, because it still counts
Only write it if it is practical
quiz.explain: Silly ideas keep the flow going and often lead to useful ones. Judging comes after the list is finished.

lessons.title: Mix and remix: combining ideas
lessons.content:
Many fresh ideas come from connecting two things that do not normally go together. A phone plus a camera became the smartphone camera. Rickshaw art took a vehicle and turned it into a moving gallery. Your job is to make these unexpected connections on purpose.

One simple method is random-word pairing. Pick your topic, then pick a random word, for example by opening a book to any page. Ask how that word could change your topic. A "school bag" and "umbrella" might lead to a bag with a pop-out rain cover.

Another tool is SCAMPER, a list of prompts: Substitute, Combine, Adapt, Modify, Put to another use, Eliminate and Reverse. Run an object through a few of these questions, like "What could I remove?" or "What if I flipped it?", and new versions start to appear.
key_points: New ideas often come from connecting unrelated things.
Random-word pairing forces unexpected connections.
SCAMPER gives you seven prompts to remix any object or idea.
lessons.tip: You do not need all seven SCAMPER prompts every time. Two or three good questions are often enough to spark something new.
lessons.task: Take an everyday object like a tiffin box. Use three SCAMPER prompts, for example Combine, Eliminate and Reverse, and sketch or describe one redesign for each.

quiz.q: What does random-word pairing help you do?
options: Make unexpected connections between unrelated things
quiz.explain: Pairing your topic with a random word pushes your mind to link things it would not normally connect.

quiz.q: In SCAMPER, what does the "E" stand for?
quiz.explain: E is Eliminate: ask what you could remove or simplify. Taking something away can create a surprisingly new version.

quiz.q: Which is an example of the "Combine" prompt?
options: Using a tiffin box as a plant pot
Adding a small cooler compartment to a tiffin box
Turning a tiffin box upside down
quiz.explain: Combine means joining two things or functions into one, like a lunch box and a cooler.

lessons.title: Capture ideas before they vanish
lessons.content:
Ideas rarely arrive when you sit down and wait for them. They show up in the shower, on a bus, during a walk or just before sleep, when your mind is relaxed and wandering. The problem is that they leave just as quickly, often within minutes.

The fix is simple: always have one capture place. It can be a small notebook in your bag or a single note on your phone. What matters is that it is always within reach and that you use only one, so you never have to wonder where an idea went.

Capture fast and rough. A few words or a quick sketch is enough to bring the idea back later. Once a week, read through your notes. Some ideas will look weak, but a few will connect with each other or with a new problem, and that is where real projects begin.
key_points: Ideas often come at odd, relaxed moments and fade quickly.
Keep one capture place that is always within reach.
Write ideas quickly and review them once a week.
lessons.tip: Pin your idea note to the top of your phone's notes app, or keep a pen clipped to your notebook, so capturing takes less than ten seconds.
lessons.task: Choose one capture place today, a notebook or a phone note. For the next three days, write down every idea that comes to you, however small or strange.

quiz.q: Why do you need a capture system for ideas?
options: Ideas often arrive at odd moments and fade within minutes
Ideas only come when you sit at a desk
Writing ideas down makes them perfect
It is required before you can start any project
quiz.explain: Ideas show up when your mind wanders and disappear fast, so you need a quick way to keep them.

quiz.q: What makes a good capture place?
options: Many different notebooks for different moods
A beautiful journal you only use at home
One place that is always within reach
Your memory, if you try hard enough
quiz.explain: One place that is always nearby means you capture ideas quickly and always know where to find them.

quiz.q: Why review your idea notes once a week?
options: To delete everything and start fresh
To spot ideas that connect or fit a new problem
To count how many ideas you had
quiz.explain: Looking back helps you notice links between ideas, and those links often turn into real projects.

lessons.title: Why creative block happens
lessons.content:
Creative block is not a sign that you have run out of talent. It is usually a signal that something specific is in the way. Once you can name the cause, you can usually work around it, and the block shrinks from a wall into a small hurdle.

Four causes show up again and again. Perfectionism makes every first attempt feel not good enough, so you never start. Fear of judgment makes you imagine what others will say before you have made anything. An empty input tank means you have not seen, read or heard anything new in a while, so there is little to combine. And too many options leave you frozen, because when you can make anything, choosing one thing feels impossible.

Each cause has its own fix. Perfectionism eases when you lower the stakes and call it a draft. Fear eases when you make something just for yourself first. An empty tank needs fresh input, and too many options need a limit. The next lessons cover these fixes one by one.
key_points: Creative block has specific causes, not a lack of talent.
The common causes are perfectionism, fear of judgment, an empty input tank and too many options.
Naming the cause tells you which fix to try.
lessons.tip: When you feel stuck, ask yourself one question: am I scared, empty or overwhelmed? The answer points straight to the cause.
lessons.task: Think of the last time you got stuck on something creative, like a post, a drawing or a school project. Write two lines about what happened and name which of the four causes was behind it.

quiz.q: What is creative block usually a sign of?
options: Something specific is getting in the way
quiz.explain: Block usually has a specific cause, such as perfectionism or fear. Naming it is the first step to getting past it.

quiz.q: Riya keeps rewriting the first line of her story because it never feels good enough. Which cause is this?
quiz.explain: Never being satisfied with a first attempt is classic perfectionism. Calling it a draft lowers the stakes.

quiz.q: Which fix matches the cause 'too many options'?
options: Show your work to more people
Set a limit, such as one topic or one colour
quiz.explain: When everything is possible, choosing is hard. A limit narrows the choices so you can start.

lessons.title: Constraints make you more creative
lessons.content:
It sounds backwards, but limits often make ideas better. A blank page with no rules gives your brain nothing to push against. A rule like 'only three colours' or 'finish in 15 minutes' gives you a puzzle to solve, and puzzles get the mind moving.

Constraints come in many forms. A time limit stops you from overthinking. A materials limit, such as only what is on your desk, forces you to use things in unexpected ways. A format limit, such as a story in 50 words or a photo from one spot, makes you choose what really matters. Many famous works came from tight limits, from six-word stories to films shot on a tiny budget.

The trick is to choose your constraints on purpose. Pick one or two clear limits before you start, not ten. If you feel too free and keep stalling, add a limit. If you feel trapped and bored, swap one limit for a different one. The goal is a rule that challenges you without making the task impossible.
key_points: Limits give your brain a puzzle to solve instead of a blank page.
Useful constraints include time, materials and format.
Choose one or two clear limits before you start.
lessons.tip: Stuck on a blank page? Add one rule right now, such as a 10-minute timer or a word limit, and start before you can argue with it.
lessons.task: Set a 15-minute timer and make something using only three colours, three objects or exactly 50 words. Stop when the timer ends, even if it is not finished.

quiz.q: Why can constraints boost creativity?
options: They make the work easier to judge
They turn a blank page into a puzzle to solve
They remove the need for ideas
quiz.explain: A limit gives your mind something to push against, which sparks fresh solutions.

quiz.q: Which of these is a format constraint?
options: Using only items on your desk
Telling a story in exactly 50 words
quiz.explain: A fixed word count limits the shape of the work, which makes it a format constraint.

quiz.q: You keep stalling because you could make anything at all. What should you try?
options: Add one or two clear limits
Add ten different rules at once
quiz.explain: Too much freedom causes stalling. One or two clear limits help, while ten rules can make the task impossible.

lessons.title: Fill the well: input and curiosity
lessons.content:
Ideas do not come from nowhere. They are built from the things you have seen, heard, read and felt. If you only scroll the same feed every day, your ideas start to look like everyone else's. When the well is dry, nothing comes up, no matter how hard you pull.

Varied input refills it. Take a walk without headphones and notice sounds and shapes. Read something outside your usual interests. Talk to someone older or from a different job. Look at art forms you do not make yourself: if you write, watch dance; if you draw, listen to music. Different sources give you different pieces to combine.

Collect inspiration actively instead of waiting for it. Keep your idea notebook from Level 1 open to new input: a phrase from a conversation, a colour on a shop sign, an odd detail on the bus. Curiosity is a habit. The more you ask why something looks or works the way it does, the fuller your well becomes.
key_points: Creative output depends on the input you take in.
Variety matters: walks, books, conversations and other art forms.
Collect inspiration actively and write it down.
lessons.tip: Once a week, consume one thing you would never normally choose, like a podcast on a strange topic or a magazine from a different field.
lessons.task: Spend 20 minutes walking or sitting in your neighbourhood without your phone screen. Write down 5 details you had never noticed before.

quiz.q: Why does scrolling the same feed every day hurt creativity?
options: It gives you the same input as everyone else
It makes you too tired to sleep
quiz.explain: Ideas are built from input. Same input leads to similar ideas, so variety helps you stand out.

quiz.q: You mostly write stories. Which input adds the most variety?
options: Reading more stories in the same genre
quiz.explain: Input from a different art form gives you new pieces to combine with your own craft.

quiz.q: What does collecting inspiration actively mean?
options: Noticing details and writing them down
quiz.explain: Active collecting means paying attention and capturing what you notice, so the details are there when you need them.

lessons.title: Make it bad on purpose
lessons.content:
The hardest part of making anything is starting, and the main reason is pressure. When you expect the first try to be good, your hand freezes. So flip the rule: try to make it bad. When the goal is a mess, there is nothing to fail at, and you start moving.

This is the idea behind the ugly first draft. A first draft exists only to get something onto the page so you have material to shape. Writers, designers and filmmakers all make rough versions that nobody sees. Playful warm-ups work the same way: a one-minute doodle with your other hand, the silliest possible headline, or a photo taken without looking at the screen.

Something surprising happens when you make it bad on purpose. Hidden inside the mess there is often one good idea, an odd angle, a funny line or an unexpected colour. Once you have started, improving a bad draft is far easier than creating a perfect one from nothing.
key_points: Aiming for bad removes the pressure that stops you starting.
An ugly first draft is raw material, not a final piece.
Bad versions often hide one good idea worth keeping.
lessons.tip: Name your file or page 'ugly draft'. That one word gives you permission to make mistakes.
lessons.task: Deliberately make the worst possible version of something today: a poster, a poem, a photo or a logo. Then look at it and write down one good idea hiding in it.

quiz.q: Why does trying to make something bad help you start?
options: It removes the pressure of getting it right
quiz.explain: When the goal is a mess, there is nothing to fail at, so the freeze goes away and you begin.

quiz.q: What is the main job of an ugly first draft?
options: To give you material to shape
quiz.explain: A first draft just gets something on the page. You improve it later.

quiz.q: Which is a playful warm-up?
options: Reading reviews of your old work
Doodling for one minute with your other hand
Planning a project for an hour
quiz.explain: A short, silly exercise lowers the stakes and gets your hands moving.

lessons.title: Learn to see light
lessons.content:
Photography literally means drawing with light. Before you think about the subject, look at the light falling on it. The same cup of cha can look warm and cosy or flat and boring, and the only thing that changed is the light. Your phone camera is good enough; what matters is noticing.

Start with direction. Light from the front flattens a face or object. Light from the side shows texture and shape, because it creates shadows. Light from behind gives a glowing outline or a silhouette. Then look at softness: a cloudy sky or a window with a thin curtain gives soft light with gentle shadows, while harsh midday sun gives hard, sharp shadows.

Time of day changes everything. The hour after sunrise and before sunset is called golden hour: the light is low, warm and soft, and almost anything looks beautiful. Midday light is strong and from above, which is harder to work with. When a photo feels dull, try moving yourself, the object or the time before you change anything else.
key_points: Light direction (front, side, back) changes shape and mood.
Soft light gives gentle shadows; hard light gives sharp ones.
Golden hour, just after sunrise and before sunset, gives warm, flattering light.
lessons.tip: Before you take a photo, ask one question: where is the light coming from? Just asking it will improve your pictures more than any new phone.
lessons.task: Pick one simple object, like a mug or a fruit. Photograph it three times today: near a window, under a ceiling light and outside. Put the three photos side by side and write one line on how the mood changed.

quiz.q: Which light direction best shows the texture of an object?
options: Light from the camera flash only
quiz.explain: Side light creates small shadows across the surface, which reveals texture and shape.

quiz.q: What is golden hour?
options: Any hour you use a yellow filter
The time just after sunrise and before sunset
quiz.explain: Around sunrise and sunset the sun is low, so the light is warm, soft and flattering.

quiz.q: A cloudy sky usually gives what kind of light?
quiz.explain: Clouds spread the sunlight out, like a giant curtain, so shadows become soft and gentle.

lessons.title: Composition: the rule of thirds and leading lines
lessons.content:
Composition is how you arrange things inside the frame. Most beginners put the subject right in the centre, every time. That is not wrong, but it often feels static. A simple guide called the rule of thirds helps: imagine the frame split by two horizontal and two vertical lines into nine equal boxes.

Place your subject on one of those lines, or where two lines cross, instead of in the middle. Put the horizon on the top or bottom line, not across the centre. Leave a little space in the direction a person is looking or a rickshaw is moving. Most phone cameras can show these grid lines; turn the grid on in the camera settings.

Leading lines are lines in the scene that pull the viewer's eye toward your subject: a road, a railway track, a riverbank, a row of lamp posts, even the edge of a table. When a line starts near the corner of the frame and travels toward the subject, the eye follows it naturally. Combine the two ideas and even an ordinary street becomes a strong photo.
key_points: The rule of thirds splits the frame into nine boxes with four lines.
Placing subjects off-centre on those lines often feels more alive.
Leading lines like roads or rails guide the eye to the subject.
lessons.tip: Rules are starting points, not laws. Once you can use the thirds grid on purpose, you can also break it on purpose, for example with a perfectly centred, symmetrical shot.
lessons.task: Turn on the grid in your phone camera. Take three photos today with the subject on a grid line or crossing point, and make sure one of them has a clear leading line, like a road, a wall or a railing, pointing toward the subject.

quiz.q: Where does the rule of thirds suggest placing the horizon?
options: Along the top or bottom grid line
quiz.explain: Putting the horizon on the upper or lower third gives more space to either the sky or the ground and avoids a split, static look.

quiz.q: What does a leading line do in a photo?
options: It guides the viewer's eye toward the subject
quiz.explain: Lines like roads or rails act like arrows, pulling the eye through the frame to what matters.

quiz.q: A person in your photo is looking to the right. Where should you leave more empty space?
options: On the right side, where they are looking
quiz.explain: Leaving space in the direction someone looks or moves makes the photo feel balanced and natural.

lessons.title: Framing, angles and negative space
lessons.content:
Most photos are taken from the same place: standing, phone at eye level. That is exactly why they look ordinary. The fastest way to make a simple scene interesting is to change your angle. Crouch down low and a cat becomes a giant. Shoot from above and a plate of food becomes a neat pattern. Move closer, then step back. Every change gives a new picture.

Framing means using something in the scene to make a frame around your subject: a doorway, a window, an arch, tree branches or even the gap between two people. A natural frame adds depth and pulls attention to what is inside it, as if you are giving the viewer a peek into a small world.

Negative space is the empty area around your subject, like plain sky, a bare wall or calm water. Beginners try to fill every corner, but empty space lets the subject breathe and stand out. One small boat on a wide, quiet river often says more than a crowded scene. Before you shoot, ask what you can remove from the frame, not just what you can add.
key_points: Changing height and angle turns ordinary scenes into fresh ones.
Natural frames like doorways and windows add depth and focus.
Negative space lets the subject stand out and breathe.
lessons.tip: Take the obvious shot first, then take five more by moving: lower, higher, closer, further, from the side. The best photo is rarely the first one.
lessons.task: Choose one ordinary subject at home, like a plant, a shoe or a kettle. Photograph it from five different angles or positions, including one very low and one from above. Pick the strongest shot and write why it works.

quiz.q: What is negative space in a photo?
options: The empty area around the subject
The part of the photo you crop out
quiz.explain: Negative space is the calm, empty area around the subject, which helps it stand out.

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of a natural frame?
options: A filter added in an editing app
A photo printed in a wooden frame
A doorway around a person standing in a room
quiz.explain: Doorways, windows and arches inside the scene frame the subject and add depth.

quiz.q: Why does shooting from a low angle often make a photo more interesting?
options: It always makes the photo sharper
It shows the scene from a view people rarely see
quiz.explain: We usually see the world from standing height, so a low angle feels fresh and can make subjects look bigger or stronger.

lessons.title: Colour and contrast
lessons.content:
Colour is often the first thing a viewer notices, even before the subject. Colours carry feeling: reds and oranges feel warm, energetic or urgent, while blues and greens feel calm and cool. When you choose what to include in a frame, you are also choosing the mood.

Contrast is difference, and difference grabs attention. Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the colour wheel, like red and green, blue and orange, or yellow and purple, and they make each other look stronger. Contrast also comes from light against dark: a bright face in a shadowy doorway, or a dark silhouette against a glowing sky.

One of the simplest tricks is a single colour accent. A red rickshaw against a grey wall, a yellow umbrella in a crowd of black ones, a green leaf on a brown floor. When most of the frame is quiet and one spot is bold, the eye goes straight to it. Look for scenes where one colour stands alone, and you will start seeing photos everywhere on your daily route.
key_points: Warm colours feel energetic; cool colours feel calm.
Complementary colours and light-against-dark create strong contrast.
A single bold colour in a quiet scene draws the eye instantly.
lessons.tip: To check contrast between light and dark, squint at the scene. The details disappear and you will clearly see which areas are bright and which are dark.
lessons.task: On your way somewhere today, look for one scene built on strong colour contrast, like a red rickshaw against a grey wall or a blue door on a yellow building. Photograph it and note which two colours or tones are doing the work.

quiz.q: Which pair are complementary colours?
quiz.explain: Blue and orange sit opposite each other on the colour wheel, so they make each other look more vivid.

quiz.q: What feeling do cool colours like blue and green usually create?
quiz.explain: Cool colours are linked with sky, water and nature, so they tend to feel calm and relaxed.

quiz.q: Why does a single colour accent work so well?
options: The eye jumps to the one bold spot in a quiet frame
It works only in black and white photos
quiz.explain: When the rest of the frame is muted, one strong colour stands out and becomes the clear centre of attention.

lessons.title: Every story needs a change
lessons.content:
A list of events is not yet a story. 'I woke up, had breakfast and went to class' tells us what happened, but nothing moves us. A story starts when someone wants something. That someone is your character, and it can be you, a friend, a shopkeeper or even a stray cat.

Next comes an obstacle: something that stands between the character and what they want. The bus is late, the rain starts, the exam is harder than expected. The obstacle creates tension, and tension is what makes people keep reading, watching or listening.

Finally, something changes by the end. The character gets what they wanted, loses it, or learns that they wanted something else. The change does not have to be big. A small shift in feeling, like going from annoyed to grateful, is enough to turn a plain moment into a story.
key_points: A story needs a character who wants something.
An obstacle creates tension and keeps people interested.
Something must change by the end, even if it is small.
lessons.tip: When a story feels flat, ask: what does the character want, and what is in the way? The answer usually shows what is missing.
lessons.task: Pick one moment from your own week and describe it in exactly three sentences: what you wanted, what got in the way, and what changed.

quiz.q: What turns a list of events into a story?
options: A character who wants something, an obstacle and a change
Writing it in the past tense
quiz.explain: Want, obstacle and change give events a shape and a reason to care.

quiz.q: What does the obstacle add to a story?
quiz.explain: When something stands in the way, the audience wants to know what happens next.

quiz.q: How big does the change at the end need to be?
options: It must change the whole world
There should be no change at all
It can be small, like a shift in feeling
quiz.explain: Even a small change, like going from annoyed to grateful, completes a story.

lessons.title: Story structure: beginning, middle, end
lessons.content:
Most stories, from a social media post to a short film, follow three parts. The beginning introduces the character and what they want. The middle brings the obstacle and the struggle. The end shows the change. This simple shape works because it matches how people naturally follow events.

The beginning needs a hook: a first line or first image that makes people curious. Start close to the action instead of with background. 'The rickshaw stopped in the middle of the flooded road' pulls you in faster than 'It was a normal Tuesday.' In the middle, build toward a turning point, the moment where things could go either way.

The end should feel clear, not cut off. A good closing line or image answers the question the hook raised, or leaves the audience with one thought to carry away. If you are not sure how to end, look back at your beginning: strong endings often echo the opening in a changed way.
key_points: Beginning sets up the want, the middle brings the struggle, the end shows the change.
Open with a hook that starts close to the action.
End with a clear closing line that answers or echoes the opening.
lessons.tip: Write your ending first. When you know where the story lands, it is much easier to choose the right hook and turning point.
lessons.task: Outline a one-minute story in three lines: a hook to open, a turning point in the middle, and a closing line.

quiz.q: What is the main job of the middle of a story?
options: Bringing the obstacle and building to a turning point
quiz.explain: The middle is where the struggle happens and the story reaches its turning point.

quiz.q: Which opening line is the stronger hook?
options: Let me tell you some background first.
This story is about my day.
The rickshaw stopped in the middle of the flooded road.
quiz.explain: Starting close to the action makes people curious right away.

quiz.q: You are not sure how to end your story. What can help?
options: Stop wherever you run out of time
Look back at the beginning and echo it in a changed way
Leave the turning point unresolved and say nothing more
quiz.explain: Endings that echo the opening feel complete and show what changed.

lessons.title: Show, don't tell
lessons.content:
'She was angry' tells the reader a fact. 'She put the cup down so hard that the cha spilled' lets the reader see it and feel it. Showing means using actions, details and senses so the audience works out the feeling themselves. That small act of figuring it out makes the story feel alive.

To show, ask what the feeling looks like from the outside. What does the person do with their hands? What do they say, or avoid saying? What can you hear, smell or touch in the scene? One or two concrete details, like a shaking voice or an untouched plate of food, are stronger than a paragraph of explanation.

Telling is not always wrong. Use it to move quickly through parts that do not matter, like 'Three days passed.' Save showing for the important moments, where you want the audience to slow down and feel something with your character.
key_points: Showing uses actions, details and senses instead of naming feelings.
One or two concrete details beat a long explanation.
Tell to move quickly; show for the moments that matter.
lessons.tip: Search your draft for feeling words like happy, sad, scared or nervous. Try replacing each one with an action or detail.
lessons.task: Rewrite 'I was nervous' as two or three sentences that show the feeling without using the word nervous.

quiz.q: Which sentence shows rather than tells?
options: He was happy about the result.
His eyes kept closing as he read the same line again.
quiz.explain: The action lets the reader see the tiredness without naming it.

quiz.q: Why does showing make a story more vivid?
options: The audience works out the feeling themselves
quiz.explain: Figuring out the feeling from details makes the audience part of the story.

quiz.q: When is telling useful?
options: Never, it should always be avoided
To move quickly through parts that do not matter
quiz.explain: Telling, like 'Three days passed', saves time so showing can shine in key moments.

lessons.title: Visual storytelling: a story in photos
lessons.content:
You already know how to compose a strong photo, and now you know how a story works. Put them together and a few pictures can tell a whole story without words. A photo story is a short sequence of images, usually 3 to 5, that moves from a beginning to an end.

A simple sequence uses three kinds of shots. The opening shot is wide and sets the scene: where are we and who is here? The detail shot moves close to show the action or emotion, like hands pouring cha or steam rising from a cup. The closing shot shows the result or the change, like a friend smiling as they take the first sip.

Plan before you shoot. Write down the moment you want to capture and list the shots you need in order. Then keep the look consistent: similar light and colour make the photos feel like one story rather than a random album. Finally, lay them out in sequence and check that someone else could follow the story without explanation.
key_points: A photo story is 3 to 5 images that move from beginning to end.
Use an opening wide shot, a close detail shot and a closing shot.
Plan the shots in order and keep light and colour consistent.
lessons.tip: Show your sequence to someone without saying anything. If they can tell you what happened, your story works.
lessons.task: Plan a 3 to 5 photo story about one small everyday event, like making cha. Write the shot list in order, then shoot it if you can.

quiz.q: What is the job of the opening shot in a photo story?
options: To set the scene and show where we are
To show only a small detail
To add text to the story
quiz.explain: A wide opening shot gives the viewer context before the story moves closer.

quiz.q: Which is a good detail shot for a story about making cha?
options: A wide shot of the whole street
Hands pouring cha with steam rising
A photo of a random sign
quiz.explain: A close detail shot shows the action and pulls the viewer into the moment.

quiz.q: Why keep light and colour consistent across the photos?
options: It makes the photos load faster
It makes them feel like one connected story
It is required by every phone camera
quiz.explain: A consistent look ties the images together so they read as one story.

lessons.title: Share your work before it feels ready
lessons.content:
Most creative work never gets shared because it never feels ready. There is always one more edit, one better photo, one cleaner line. Waiting for perfect usually means waiting forever, and work kept in a drawer cannot teach you anything.

Sharing early gives you something practice alone cannot: a reaction. When someone smiles, asks a question or looks confused, you learn what your work actually does to people. Each share also makes the next one easier, because the fear shrinks every time nothing terrible happens.

You do not need a big audience to start. One friend, a family group chat or a small online community is enough. Small audiences are kinder, give more honest feedback and let you grow without pressure. Treat each share as an experiment, not a final verdict on your talent.
key_points: Waiting for perfect usually means never sharing.
Sharing gives you real reactions that solo practice cannot.
Start with a small, friendly audience and grow from there.
lessons.tip: Before you share, decide what 'done enough' means, such as 'one round of edits'. When you reach it, share, even if it still feels a little rough.
lessons.task: Pick one piece you made in this course, like a photo, a sketch or a short story, and share it with at least one person today. Note how they reacted and how you felt afterwards.

quiz.q: Why is waiting until your work feels perfect a problem?
options: The feeling of 'ready' rarely comes, so the work never gets shared
quiz.explain: There is always one more thing to fix. If you wait to feel ready, you may never share, and you miss the learning that comes from real reactions.

quiz.q: What does sharing early give you that practising alone does not?
options: Real reactions that show what your work does to people
quiz.explain: Other people's reactions show you what lands and what confuses. You cannot get that information by working in private.

quiz.q: What is a good first audience for your work?
options: A small, friendly group like one friend or a family chat
Nobody until you are an expert
quiz.explain: Small audiences feel safer, give more honest feedback and let you build confidence step by step.

lessons.title: Handle creative critique
lessons.content:
When you ask 'Do you like it?', you usually get a polite 'Yes, nice'. That feels good but teaches you nothing. Useful feedback starts with specific questions, such as 'Where did your eye go first?', 'Which part felt slow?' or 'What do you think this story is about?'

Not every comment is equally useful. Some feedback is about taste: 'I just don't like the colour yellow.' Other feedback is about whether the work does what you intended: 'I didn't notice the person in the photo.' Taste comments tell you about the viewer. Notes about your intention tell you what to fix.

Critique should sharpen your voice, not replace it. Listen fully, say thank you, and do not argue in the moment. Later, decide calmly which notes serve your goal and which you will leave. If several people point to the same spot, that spot probably needs work.
key_points: Ask specific questions to get useful feedback.
Separate personal taste from notes about your intention.
Listen, thank, then decide later which notes to use.
lessons.tip: Write down feedback word for word while you listen. Reading it the next day, with less emotion, makes it much easier to judge fairly.
lessons.task: Choose one piece you made and write three specific questions you would ask someone about it, like 'What did you notice first?'. Ask at least one person today if you can.

quiz.q: Which question is most likely to get useful feedback?
options: Where did your eye go first in this photo?
quiz.explain: Specific questions point the viewer at something concrete, so their answer tells you exactly what is working or not.

quiz.q: 'I just don't like yellow' is an example of...
quiz.explain: This tells you about the viewer's preference, not whether your work achieved its goal. You can note it and move on.

quiz.q: What should you do right after receiving critique?
options: Stop making that kind of work
Listen, thank them and decide later which notes to use
quiz.explain: Arguing stops people from being honest, and changing everything loses your voice. Calm reflection later helps you keep the useful notes.

lessons.title: Originality, influence and credit
lessons.content:
Every creator learns by studying others. Musicians copy songs to practise, painters sketch old masters, writers imitate authors they love. Influence is normal. The difference between learning and copying is what you do next: do you take the whole thing, or do you take a lesson from it?

A useful habit is to borrow techniques, not finished work. Notice how a photographer uses light, how a writer opens a story, or how a designer pairs colours. Then mix that technique with your own subject, your own place and your own experience. Combining several influences, instead of copying just one, is how a personal style grows.

When you use someone else's actual work, such as a photo, a song or a quote, give clear credit and ask permission when it is not yours to use. Respecting other creators protects them, builds trust and shows that you understand how creative communities work.
key_points: Learning from others is normal; copying whole works is not.
Borrow techniques and mix several influences into your own style.
Credit others and ask permission before using their work.
lessons.tip: Keep a 'steal list' of techniques you admire, with the creator's name next to each one. It trains your eye and keeps your credits honest.
lessons.task: Choose one creator you admire. List two specific things you could borrow from them, like their use of light or their way of opening a story, and one way to make each your own.

quiz.q: What is the healthiest way to learn from an artist you admire?
options: Copy their work and post it as yours
Borrow their techniques and mix them with your own ideas
Avoid looking at other people's work
quiz.explain: Studying techniques is how every creator grows. Mixing them with your own subject and experience turns influence into originality.

quiz.q: How does a personal style usually develop?
options: By combining many influences with your own experience
quiz.explain: When many influences blend with your own life and choices, the result becomes something only you could make.

quiz.q: You want to use another person's photo in your project. What should you do?
options: Use it, since it is online anyway
Crop it so nobody recognises it
Change the colours and call it yours
Ask permission and give clear credit
quiz.explain: Being online does not make work free to use. Asking permission and crediting the creator respects their work and builds trust.

lessons.title: Build a creative practice that lasts
lessons.content:
Inspiration is unreliable, but habits are not. Creators who keep going usually have a small ritual: ten minutes of sketching with morning cha, one photo on the walk home, a page of writing before bed. A small, regular practice beats rare bursts of big effort.

A project gives your practice direction. A 30-day challenge works well: one simple task each day, kept under 15 minutes, like 'one photo of something blue' or 'a six-word story'. Keep the rules clear and the task small, so a busy or low-energy day does not break the chain. If you miss a day, simply continue the next day.

Finally, learn to finish. Unfinished projects quietly drain confidence. Set a clear finish line before you start, accept 'good enough' when you reach it, and celebrate completing things. Each finished piece, even a tiny one, proves to you that you are a person who makes things.
key_points: Small regular habits beat rare bursts of inspiration.
A 30-day challenge with tiny daily tasks builds momentum.
Set a clear finish line and finish what you start.
lessons.tip: Attach your creative habit to something you already do every day, like drinking tea or commuting. The existing habit becomes your reminder.
lessons.task: Design your own 30-day creative challenge: choose a theme, write a daily task that takes under 15 minutes, decide when you will do it, and complete day one today.

quiz.q: Why is a small daily habit better than waiting for inspiration?
options: Inspiration is unreliable, but habits keep you making regularly
Small work is always better than big work
Habits remove the need for ideas
quiz.explain: Inspiration comes and goes. A regular habit means you keep practising on ordinary days, which is where most growth happens.

quiz.q: What makes a 30-day challenge easier to stick to?
options: Making each task take at least two hours
Keeping each daily task small and clear, under 15 minutes
Quitting after the first missed day
quiz.explain: Small, clear tasks fit even busy days. If you miss one, continue the next day instead of giving up.

quiz.q: How can you get better at finishing projects?
options: Start several new projects at once
Set a clear finish line before you begin and accept 'good enough'
Keep editing until it is perfect
Only work when you feel inspired
quiz.explain: A clear finish line tells you when you are done. Accepting 'good enough' stops endless polishing and builds the habit of completing.

categories.name: Computer Science
categories.tagline: Every BSc and MSc CSE course, explained like a friend would.
categories.description: One lesson per university course, from your first C program to your MSc thesis. Each one tells you what it is, why it matters, how it works and where you see it in real life.

messages.welcome: Hey! Forget the heavy textbooks for a bit. We'll go through the whole CSE degree one course at a time, with simple words and real examples.
messages.comeback: Your next course is waiting. Just read the first paragraph, that's all. You'll want to keep going.
messages.pass: Nice! You actually get this course now, not just the name.
messages.fail: No worries, even toppers miss questions. Read the explanations, look at the lesson again and try once more.
messages.finished: You just walked through the whole BSc and MSc in CSE: programming, math, hardware, systems, networks, AI and the future tech. Pick the course you liked most and build one small project with it.

lessons.title: Introduction to Computer Systems
lessons.content:
What is it? This is the 'hello, computer' course. It shows you what a computer actually is: a machine that takes input, processes it, stores it and gives you output. You meet the main parts: the CPU (the brain), memory or RAM (the desk where work happens right now), storage like a hard disk or SSD (the cupboard where things are kept for later), and input and output devices like the keyboard, mouse and screen.

Why learn it? Every other course in computer science sits on top of this one. If you don't know the difference between RAM and storage, or between hardware and software, the later courses feel like magic. This course turns the magic into simple, understandable parts.

How does it work? First you learn the input, process, output cycle. Then you learn that computers only understand 0 and 1, called binary, and that eight of those bits make a byte. You learn what an operating system does (it is the manager that lets apps share the hardware), what software and apps are, how files and folders are stored, and a little about the internet and how computers talk to each other.

Real life example: Think of a restaurant kitchen. The order slip is the input. The chef is the CPU, cooking step by step. The kitchen counter is RAM: small but fast, holding only what is being cooked right now. The fridge and store room are storage: big, slower, but things stay there even overnight. The plate that reaches your table is the output. When you open Facebook on your phone, the same thing happens: your tap is input, the CPU works, RAM holds the app, storage keeps your photos, and the screen shows the result.

Wrap-up: After this course you can explain how a computer works to anyone, read a laptop spec sheet and understand it, and you are ready to start programming in the next course.
key_points: A computer takes input, processes it, stores it and gives output.
CPU is the brain, RAM is the fast work desk, storage is the long-term cupboard.
Computers think in binary: 0s and 1s. 8 bits make 1 byte.
The operating system manages hardware so apps can share it.
lessons.tip: Open your phone or laptop settings and find the 'About' page. Match every word you see there (RAM, storage, processor) with what you learned. Real things stick better than definitions.
lessons.task: Pick any app you use daily, like bKash or YouTube. Write down one example each of input, processing, storage and output in that app.

quiz.q: Which part of a computer is often called its brain?
quiz.explain: The CPU does the actual processing and follows instructions, so it is called the brain of the computer.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between RAM and storage?
options: RAM is fast and temporary, storage keeps data even after power off
Storage is where the CPU does its math
quiz.explain: RAM is the fast work desk that is cleared when power goes off. Storage like an SSD keeps your files for later.

quiz.q: How many bits make one byte?
quiz.explain: One byte is 8 bits. Each bit is a single 0 or 1.

lessons.title: Structured Programming (C)
lessons.content:
What is it? This is usually your first real programming course, and the language is C. Structured programming means writing a program in a clean, top-to-bottom way using three simple building blocks: steps in order (sequence), choices (if and else) and repeats (loops). No jumping around randomly, just tidy blocks.

Why learn it? C is old but it is everywhere: operating systems, phone chips, washing machines and even parts of Python are written in C. Because C is close to the hardware, learning it teaches you how memory and computers really work. Once you know C, picking up other languages becomes much easier.

How does it work? You learn variables (named boxes that hold values) and data types like int, float and char. You learn if-else to make decisions, and for and while loops to repeat things. You learn functions, which are small reusable machines: give them input, get output back. Then come arrays (a row of boxes), strings (text), and the famous pointers, which are just addresses telling you where something lives in memory. Finally you read and write files.

Real life example: Think of making tea. Sequence: boil water, add tea leaves, add sugar. Choice: if someone wants milk, add milk, else skip it. Loop: keep stirring while the sugar has not dissolved. A function is like asking your little brother 'make tea' and getting a cup back without explaining every step again. A pointer is like a house address: instead of carrying the whole house, you just give someone the address.

Wrap-up: After this course you can write small programs that solve real problems, like a calculator, a marks grading system or a simple game. Next you will meet Object Oriented Programming and Data Structures, which build directly on this.
key_points: Structured programming uses three blocks: sequence, choice and loops.
Variables are named boxes, functions are reusable mini machines.
Arrays hold many values in a row, strings hold text.
Pointers store memory addresses, like a house address.
lessons.tip: Type every example yourself instead of copy-pasting. Your fingers learn the syntax, and the errors you make teach you more than the book.
lessons.task: On paper, write the steps for a program that reads a student's marks and prints A, B, C or F. Use if-else for the grades and a loop to do it for 5 students.

quiz.q: What are the three building blocks of structured programming?
quiz.explain: Structured programs are built only from steps in order, choices and repeats, which keeps them easy to read.

quiz.q: What does a pointer in C store?
quiz.explain: A pointer holds the address of where some data lives in memory, like a house address.

quiz.q: Why is a function useful?
options: You can reuse the same code again and again by calling it
It makes the program run without a CPU
quiz.explain: A function packs a task into one named block, so you call it whenever needed instead of rewriting the code.

lessons.title: Discrete Mathematics
lessons.content:
What is it? Discrete maths is the maths of separate, countable things: people, phones, cities, true or false. Not smooth curves, but steps and pieces. It is the maths computers love, because computers also work with separate things: 0 or 1, yes or no.

Why learn it? This is the language of computer science. Logic helps you write correct if-conditions. Sets help with databases. Counting helps you know how many passwords are possible. Graphs help Google Maps find routes. Proofs teach you to be sure your algorithm is correct, not just hope it is.

How does it work? You start with logic: statements that are true or false, joined with AND, OR and NOT. Then sets, which are groups of things, and relations and functions between them. Then counting: permutations (order matters) and combinations (order does not matter). Then proofs, including induction, which is like dominoes: if the first one falls and each one knocks the next, they all fall. Finally graphs (dots connected by lines) and trees.

Real life example: Your Facebook friends form a graph: each person is a dot, each friendship is a line. 'People you may know' is graph thinking. A 4-digit bKash PIN has 10 x 10 x 10 x 10 = 10,000 possibilities, that is counting. Choosing 11 players from a squad of 15 for a cricket match is a combination, because the order of picking does not matter. And 'if it rains AND I have no umbrella, I stay home' is pure logic.

Wrap-up: After this course you will think more precisely, spot wrong reasoning quickly, and be ready for Algorithms, Databases and Theory of Computation, which all stand on this ground.
key_points: Discrete maths deals with separate, countable things, just like computers.
Logic (AND, OR, NOT) powers every if-condition you write.
Permutations care about order, combinations do not.
Graphs of dots and lines model friends, roads and networks.
lessons.tip: Draw everything. Sets as circles, graphs as dots and lines, logic as truth tables. A drawing makes a scary formula look friendly.
lessons.task: Draw a graph of 6 of your friends or family: dots for people, lines if they know each other. Who has the most lines? That person is the most 'connected' node.

quiz.q: Why is discrete maths important for computer science?
options: It is used for drawing pictures
Computers work with separate values like 0 and 1, just like discrete maths
quiz.explain: Computers deal with separate, countable values, and discrete maths is exactly the maths of such things.

quiz.q: Picking 11 players from 15, where order does not matter, is a...
quiz.explain: When order does not matter, it is a combination. If order mattered, it would be a permutation.

quiz.q: Proof by induction is often compared to...
quiz.explain: Show the first case is true and that each case leads to the next, and like dominoes, all cases fall into place.

lessons.title: Calculus & Differential Equations
lessons.content:
What is it? Calculus is the maths of change. It answers two big questions: how fast is something changing right now (derivatives), and how much has piled up over time (integrals). Differential equations are rules that describe how something changes, like 'this population grows faster when it is bigger'.

Why learn it? Lots of computer science uses change. Machine learning trains models using derivatives (a method called gradient descent). Games and animations use it to move things smoothly. Physics simulations, signal processing, graphics and even economics models all need calculus.

How does it work? You start with limits: what value does something get closer and closer to. Then derivatives: the slope, or speed, at a single moment. Then integrals: adding up tiny pieces to find a total area or total amount. Derivatives and integrals are opposites of each other. Finally, differential equations: you know the rule of change and you work backwards to find the full story.

Real life example: You are riding a Pathao bike. The speedometer shows 40 km/h at this very second, that is a derivative: how fast distance is changing right now. At the end of the trip, the app shows you travelled 12 km total, that is an integral: all the tiny bits of distance added up. And when a cup of hot tea cools faster when it is very hot and slower as it gets close to room temperature, that cooling rule is a differential equation.

Wrap-up: After this course you can measure change, find maximum and minimum values (like the cheapest cost or highest profit), and you will understand how AI models 'learn' later on. Linear Algebra and Numerical Methods come next.
key_points: Calculus is the maths of change.
A derivative is the speed of change at one moment.
An integral adds up tiny pieces to get a total.
Differential equations describe how something changes over time.
lessons.tip: Always ask 'what is changing, and with respect to what?' Once you say it in words, the formula becomes much easier to set up.
lessons.task: Note your phone battery percentage every 10 minutes for an hour while using it. How much does it drop per minute? You just calculated a rate of change, a derivative in real life.

quiz.q: A speedometer showing your speed right now is an example of a...
quiz.explain: A derivative tells how fast something changes at one moment, exactly what a speedometer shows.

quiz.q: What does an integral do?
options: Adds up tiny pieces to find a total
quiz.explain: An integral collects many small pieces to give a total, like total distance travelled.

quiz.q: Where is calculus used in machine learning?
options: Gradient descent uses derivatives to improve the model
It is not used at all
quiz.explain: Gradient descent uses derivatives to find which way to adjust a model so its error goes down.

lessons.title: Electrical Circuits
lessons.content:
What is it? This course is about how electricity flows through wires and parts like resistors, capacitors and inductors. Every computer is, deep down, a giant electric circuit, so CSE students learn the basics of how current moves.

Why learn it? If you want to understand hardware, build robots, work with IoT devices or design chips, you need to know why a circuit works or burns out. It also explains everyday things: why a charger gets warm, why a fuse blows, why the power supply matters.

How does it work? Three main words: voltage (the push), current (the flow) and resistance (the blocking). Ohm's law ties them together: V = I x R. You learn series circuits (one path, like a single line) and parallel circuits (many paths side by side). You learn Kirchhoff's laws: current going into a point equals current coming out, and voltages around a closed loop add up to zero. Then capacitors (tiny storage tanks for charge), inductors, and the difference between DC (battery, one direction) and AC (wall socket, back and forth).

Real life example: Think of water in a pipe. Voltage is the water pressure from the tank on the roof. Current is how much water is flowing. Resistance is a narrow part of the pipe. In your house, lights and fans are wired in parallel. That is why if one bulb fuses, the fan still runs. Old Eid fairy lights were often in series, so when one bulb died, the whole string went dark.

Wrap-up: After this course you can read simple circuit diagrams, calculate current and voltage, and you are ready for Electronic Devices and Digital Logic Design, where circuits start to think.
key_points: Voltage is the push, current is the flow, resistance blocks the flow.
Ohm's law: V = I x R.
Series has one path, parallel has many paths.
DC flows one way, AC flows back and forth.
lessons.tip: Use the water pipe picture for everything. When a formula confuses you, ask what the pressure, the flow and the narrow part are.
lessons.task: Look at a phone charger. Find the printed output, like 5V 2A. Use P = V x I to calculate its power in watts.

quiz.q: What is Ohm's law?
quiz.explain: Ohm's law says voltage equals current times resistance.

quiz.q: Why does the fan keep running when one bulb in your room fuses?
options: Because the fan has its own battery
Because house wiring is in parallel
quiz.explain: In parallel, each device has its own path, so one broken path does not stop the others.

quiz.q: Which one is AC?
options: The electricity from a wall socket
quiz.explain: Wall sockets give alternating current that switches direction many times a second. Batteries give DC.

lessons.title: Object Oriented Programming
lessons.content:
What is it? Object Oriented Programming, or OOP, is a way of organizing code around 'objects', just like the real world is full of objects. A car, a student, a bank account: each has data (what it has) and behaviour (what it can do). OOP courses usually use Java, C++ or Python.

Why learn it? Big programs get messy fast. OOP keeps code tidy by putting related data and actions together. Almost every big app you use, from Android apps to games to banking software, is built with OOP ideas. Job interviews ask about it all the time.

How does it work? A class is a blueprint, an object is a real thing made from it. Then there are four big ideas. Encapsulation: hide the inside details and give only safe buttons to press. Inheritance: a child class gets everything from a parent class and can add more. Polymorphism: the same command behaves differently for different objects. Abstraction: show only what matters, hide the complicated stuff.

Real life example: 'Mobile phone' is a class, the blueprint. Your Samsung and your friend's iPhone are objects made from that idea. Encapsulation: you press the power button, you don't touch the circuit board. Inheritance: a 'smartphone' class inherits calling from 'phone' and adds a camera and apps. Polymorphism: you say 'make a sound' to a cat object and it says meow, to a dog object and it says woof. Same command, different result. A bKash account object has a balance hidden inside, and you can only change it through safe methods like sendMoney or cashOut.

Wrap-up: After this course you can design programs as a team of objects, write cleaner and reusable code, and you are ready for Software Engineering and design patterns.
key_points: A class is a blueprint, an object is a real thing built from it.
Encapsulation hides inside details behind safe methods.
Inheritance lets a child class reuse a parent's features.
Polymorphism means one command, different behaviour per object.
lessons.tip: Before coding, look around your room and turn things into classes on paper: what data does a fan have, and what can it do? This trains the OOP eye.
lessons.task: Design a 'Student' class on paper: list 4 pieces of data (like name, roll) and 3 actions (like study, giveExam). Then make a 'CSEStudent' class that inherits it and adds one new action.

quiz.q: What is the relationship between a class and an object?
options: A class is a blueprint, an object is made from it
A class is a type of loop
quiz.explain: A class describes what something should be like. An object is one real copy built from that description.

quiz.q: Hiding a bank balance and only allowing changes through safe methods is called...
quiz.explain: Encapsulation keeps data private and exposes only safe ways to use it.

quiz.q: A cat says meow and a dog says woof to the same 'makeSound' command. This is...
quiz.explain: Polymorphism means one command can behave differently depending on the object.

lessons.title: Data Structures
lessons.content:
What is it? A data structure is a way to arrange data so you can use it quickly. Just like you keep clothes in a wardrobe, books on a shelf and spices in a rack, programs keep data in different shapes depending on what they need to do with it.

Why learn it? The right structure can make a program thousands of times faster. Facebook, Google and Daraz handle millions of items every second, and they can only do it because they pick smart data structures. This is also the number one topic in programming job interviews.

How does it work? Array: boxes in a row, super fast if you know the position number. Linked list: each item holds a pointer to the next, easy to insert in the middle. Stack: last in, first out, like a pile of plates. Queue: first in, first out, like a line at the bank. Tree: a family-tree shape, great for searching and folders. Heap: a tree that always keeps the biggest or smallest on top. Hash table: jump straight to an item using a key, like a dictionary. Graph: dots and lines for networks and maps. You also learn Big O, a way to say how fast something is as data grows.

Real life example: The undo button in MS Word is a stack: the last thing you did is undone first. The ticket line at a cinema is a queue. The folders on your computer form a tree. Your phone's contact search is like a hash table: type the name and the number pops up instantly. Google Maps uses a graph of roads. And the hospital emergency room is a heap: the most serious patient goes first, not the one who came first.

Wrap-up: After this course you can choose the right structure for any problem and explain why, and you are ready for Algorithms, which uses these structures as its tools.
key_points: A data structure is a smart way to arrange data for fast use.
Stack is last-in-first-out, queue is first-in-first-out.
Trees, hash tables and graphs power search, lookup and maps.
Big O tells how speed changes as data grows.
lessons.tip: Draw boxes and arrows for every operation: push, pop, insert, delete. If you can draw it, you can code it.
lessons.task: Find three examples at home or outside of a stack, a queue and a tree. Write them down with one line each on why they fit.

quiz.q: The undo button in a text editor works like a...
quiz.explain: Undo removes the last action first, which is last in, first out, exactly a stack.

quiz.q: A line of people at a bank counter is a...
quiz.explain: Whoever comes first gets served first, which is first in, first out, a queue.

quiz.q: What does Big O notation describe?
options: How running time grows as the data grows
