quiz.explain: Big O describes how the time or memory a program needs grows when the input gets bigger.

lessons.title: Digital Logic Design
lessons.content:
What is it? Digital Logic Design, or DLD, shows how a computer makes decisions using only 0 and 1. Tiny electronic switches called logic gates take 0s and 1s in and give a 0 or 1 out. By joining millions of gates, we build adders, memory and finally a whole CPU.

Why learn it? This is the bridge between electricity and programming. When you write 'if a and b', somewhere in the chip an AND gate is doing that. Chip designers, embedded engineers and computer architects all need DLD, and it makes every later hardware course easy.

How does it work? First, number systems: binary, octal, hexadecimal and how to convert between them. Then the basic gates: AND (both must be 1), OR (at least one is 1), NOT (flips it), plus NAND, NOR and XOR. Boolean algebra lets you simplify gate circuits, and K-maps are a neat picture trick for that. Combinational circuits like adders, multiplexers and decoders give output based only on current input. Sequential circuits like flip-flops, registers and counters also remember the past, which is how memory is born.

Real life example: A bike that starts only if the key is turned AND the kickstand is up is an AND gate. A room light that you can switch on from either of two switches works like an OR gate. A calculator adding 5 + 3 uses an adder circuit made of gates. And a digital clock counting seconds uses a counter made of flip-flops, which remembers the last number and adds one.

Wrap-up: After this course you can design small digital circuits, simplify them, and you will see exactly how numbers get added inside a chip. Computer Architecture and Microprocessors come next.
key_points: Logic gates take 0s and 1s and output a 0 or 1.
AND needs both, OR needs at least one, NOT flips the value.
Boolean algebra and K-maps simplify circuits.
Combinational circuits don't remember, sequential circuits do.
lessons.tip: Make a truth table for every circuit before you trust it. Write all input combinations and check each output. It catches mistakes fast.
lessons.task: Write the truth table for 'I go out if it is NOT raining AND my homework is done'. Two inputs, four rows.

quiz.q: An AND gate gives 1 when...
quiz.explain: AND outputs 1 only when all its inputs are 1.

quiz.q: Which circuit can remember a value?
quiz.explain: A flip-flop is a sequential circuit that stores one bit, the basic unit of memory.

quiz.q: What is a K-map used for?
quiz.explain: Karnaugh maps are a visual way to simplify Boolean expressions so the circuit needs fewer gates.

lessons.title: Electronic Devices & Circuits
lessons.content:
What is it? This course is about the small electronic parts that make modern gadgets possible: diodes, transistors and amplifiers. These are made from semiconductors, special materials like silicon that can either let electricity pass or block it, depending on how you treat them.

Why learn it? A transistor is the basic switch inside every chip. A modern phone processor has billions of them. If you want to understand how a CPU is physically built, why chips heat up, or how sensors and chargers work, this is where it starts.

How does it work? First, semiconductors and how adding a tiny bit of other material (doping) makes N-type and P-type silicon. Join them and you get a diode, a one-way gate for current. Diodes help turn AC into DC in chargers, and LEDs are diodes that glow. Then transistors, like BJT and MOSFET: a small signal controls a big current, so they act as a switch or an amplifier. Finally op-amps and simple amplifier circuits, which make weak signals strong.

Real life example: Your phone charger takes AC from the wall and uses diodes to turn it into DC for the battery. That's a rectifier. The bulb on the charger that glows when plugged in is an LED. A microphone signal is very weak, so an amplifier made of transistors boosts it before it reaches the loudspeaker at a waz mahfil or a concert. And inside your phone, billions of MOSFETs are switching on and off to run every app.

Wrap-up: After this course you will understand the physical parts behind digital logic, read simple electronic circuits, and see how the 0s and 1s are really made of tiny switches.
key_points: Semiconductors like silicon can pass or block current.
A diode lets current flow only one way.
A transistor is a switch or amplifier controlled by a small signal.
Billions of transistors make up every modern chip.
lessons.tip: Learn each device by its job first (one-way gate, switch, booster), then the formulas. Job first, maths second.
lessons.task: Find three LEDs in your home (charger light, TV standby light, router). Write what each one is telling you.

quiz.q: What does a diode do?
options: Lets current flow in only one direction
quiz.explain: A diode is a one-way gate for current, which is why it is used to turn AC into DC.

quiz.q: What is the transistor's main job inside a chip?
options: To act as a tiny switch
quiz.explain: Inside chips, transistors act as on/off switches, which make 0s and 1s.

quiz.q: What is silicon?
quiz.explain: Silicon is a semiconductor, so we can control whether it conducts, which is perfect for switches.

lessons.title: Linear Algebra
lessons.content:
What is it? Linear algebra is the maths of lists of numbers (vectors) and tables of numbers (matrices). It teaches how to add them, multiply them and use them to transform things, like rotating, stretching or moving shapes.

Why learn it? It is the secret engine of modern computing. Every photo is a matrix of pixel numbers. Every 3D game rotates objects with matrices. Machine learning and AI are basically huge amounts of matrix multiplication. Google's original PageRank algorithm was linear algebra too.

How does it work? A vector is an arrow or a list like (3, 4). A matrix is a grid of numbers. You learn matrix addition and multiplication, and how a matrix can transform a vector. You solve systems of linear equations, like finding x and y that make two equations true, using Gaussian elimination. You learn determinants, the inverse of a matrix, vector spaces, and the famous eigenvalues and eigenvectors, which are directions that a transformation only stretches without turning.

Real life example: A black-and-white photo on your phone is a big grid of numbers, each telling how bright one pixel is. Applying a filter on Instagram is doing maths on that matrix. In a shop, if 2 shingaras and 1 tea cost 40 taka, and 1 shingara and 2 teas cost 50 taka, finding each price is solving a system of linear equations. And when you rotate a photo, the phone multiplies every point by a rotation matrix.

Wrap-up: After this course you can work with vectors and matrices, solve equation systems, and you will be ready for Computer Graphics, Machine Learning and Image Processing.
key_points: A vector is a list of numbers, a matrix is a grid of numbers.
Matrices can transform things: rotate, stretch, move.
Photos, 3D games and AI all run on matrix maths.
Eigenvectors are directions a transformation only stretches.
lessons.tip: Picture every operation. Draw arrows for vectors and see what the matrix does to them. Geometry makes linear algebra click.
lessons.task: Solve: 2 shingaras + 1 tea = 40 taka, 1 shingara + 2 teas = 50 taka. Find each price, then check your answer.

quiz.q: What is a matrix?
options: A grid of numbers in rows and columns
quiz.explain: A matrix is a rectangular table of numbers arranged in rows and columns.

quiz.q: How is a black-and-white photo stored for linear algebra?
options: As a matrix of brightness numbers
quiz.explain: Each pixel's brightness is a number, so the whole image is a matrix.

quiz.q: Which area uses huge amounts of matrix multiplication?
quiz.explain: Neural networks do layer after layer of matrix multiplication, which is why GPUs are so useful for AI.

lessons.title: Probability & Statistics
lessons.content:
What is it? Probability is the maths of chance: how likely is something to happen. Statistics is the maths of data: how to collect it, summarize it and draw honest conclusions from it.

Why learn it? The world is full of uncertainty, and computers have to deal with it. Spam filters, weather apps, recommendation systems, AI models, A/B testing in apps and data science all depend on probability and statistics. Without it, you can't tell if a result is real or just luck.

How does it work? You start with basic probability: favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes. Then conditional probability (chance of A if B already happened) and Bayes' theorem, which updates beliefs with new evidence. Then random variables and distributions, like the binomial and the famous bell-shaped normal distribution. In statistics you learn mean, median, mode, variance and standard deviation, then sampling, confidence intervals, hypothesis testing and regression, which finds a line that fits the data.

Real life example: Toss a coin: the chance of heads is 1/2. Roll a ludo dice: the chance of a 6 is 1/6. When the weather app says 70% chance of rain, that is probability. Before an election, surveyors ask a few thousand people, not everyone, and use statistics to guess the whole country's result. Gmail's spam filter asks: given this email has the words 'free prize', what is the chance it is spam? That is Bayes in action. A cricket batsman's average is the mean of his scores.

Wrap-up: After this course you can summarize data, measure uncertainty and test claims. This is the base for Machine Learning, Data Mining and every data-related job.
key_points: Probability measures chance, statistics makes sense of data.
Mean, median and standard deviation summarize data.
Bayes' theorem updates a belief with new evidence.
Samples let you learn about a whole population.
lessons.tip: Always check your answer with common sense: a probability can never be below 0 or above 1. If it is, something went wrong.
lessons.task: Write down the runs of your favourite batsman's last 10 innings (or any 10 numbers). Find the mean, median and the highest and lowest score.

quiz.q: What is the probability of rolling a 6 on a fair dice?
quiz.explain: There is 1 favourable outcome out of 6 possible ones, so the chance is 1/6.

quiz.q: Which idea does a spam filter use to update its guess based on words in an email?
quiz.explain: Bayes' theorem updates the chance an email is spam based on the evidence, like the words it contains.

quiz.q: Why do surveys ask only a sample of people?
options: Because statistics lets a good sample represent the whole population
quiz.explain: A well-chosen sample can tell us about the whole population without asking everyone.

lessons.title: Algorithms (Design & Analysis)
lessons.content:
An algorithm is just a clear set of steps to solve a problem. This course is about two things: how to design good steps, and how to measure how fast those steps are. It is like learning not just to cook, but to cook the smartest way.

Why does it matter? A slow algorithm can take hours where a smart one takes a blink. Google search, Google Maps directions, Facebook friend suggestions and even your phone's contact search all depend on clever algorithms. A faster computer helps a little. A better algorithm can help a million times more.

Here's how it works. First you learn Big-O, a way to say how the work grows when the input grows. O(n) means double the input, double the work. O(n²) means double the input, four times the work. Then you learn famous tricks: sorting (merge sort, quick sort), searching (binary search), divide and conquer (break a problem into halves), greedy (always pick the best choice right now), dynamic programming (remember answers you already found so you never redo them) and graph algorithms like shortest path.

Real life example: imagine finding a word in a dictionary. You could start from page 1 and check every word. That is linear search, slow. Or you open the middle, see if your word comes before or after, and throw away half the book each time. That is binary search. With 1,000 pages you need about 10 looks instead of 1,000. Pathao and Google Maps finding the fastest road through Dhaka traffic? That is a shortest path algorithm called Dijkstra's.

After this course you can look at a problem, pick a smart approach, and explain why it is fast. This is the heart of every coding interview and competitive programming contest. Next, practice problems on sites like Codeforces or LeetCode.
key_points: An algorithm is a step-by-step recipe for solving a problem.
Big-O tells how the work grows as the input grows.
Key techniques: divide and conquer, greedy, dynamic programming, graph algorithms.
A better algorithm often beats a faster computer.
lessons.tip: Always trace your algorithm by hand on a tiny example first, like 5 numbers. If you can't do it on paper, the code will not save you.
lessons.task: Pick a random number between 1 and 100 and ask a friend to guess it, answering only higher or lower. Count the guesses. Then show them the binary search trick: always guess the middle. Can they always win in 7 guesses?

quiz.q: What does Big-O notation describe?
options: How the work grows as the input grows
quiz.explain: Big-O measures growth. It tells you how the time or memory needed grows when the input gets bigger.

quiz.q: Binary search on 1,000 sorted items needs roughly how many checks?
quiz.explain: Binary search halves the range every step. 1,000 halves down to 1 in about 10 steps.

quiz.q: Remembering answers to small subproblems so you never solve them twice is called...
quiz.explain: Dynamic programming stores answers to subproblems and reuses them, which saves a huge amount of repeated work.

lessons.title: Computer Architecture & Organization
lessons.content:
This course opens up the computer and shows how its parts are built and how they work together. Architecture is the plan: what instructions the computer understands. Organization is the building: how the wires, chips and memory actually carry out that plan.

Why learn it? When you know what happens inside, you write faster programs and understand why one phone feels quick and another feels slow. People who design chips at Intel, Apple or ARM, and people who write games and operating systems, all use this knowledge every day.

Here's how it works. The CPU is the brain. Inside it are the ALU, which does the math, the control unit, which acts like a traffic police telling everyone what to do, and registers, tiny super-fast storage boxes. The CPU runs a simple loop forever: fetch an instruction, decode it, execute it. Memory comes in layers: registers, then cache, then RAM, then disk. Each layer is bigger but slower. You also learn pipelining, where the CPU starts the next instruction before the last one finishes, like an assembly line, and how the CPU talks to keyboards and screens through buses.

Real life example: think of a kitchen. The chef is the CPU. The cutting board right in front of him is the register, tiny but instant. The small shelf next to him is the cache. The fridge is the RAM, bigger but he has to walk to it. The bazar is the hard disk, it has everything, but going there takes ages. A smart chef keeps what he needs most close by. That is exactly why cache exists.

After this course you will understand what really happens when you press run, why memory layout affects speed, and what numbers like 3 GHz or 8 cores mean. Next stop: microprocessors and assembly, where you talk to the CPU in its own language.
key_points: The CPU repeats fetch, decode, execute forever.
ALU does math, the control unit directs, registers hold tiny fast data.
Memory is layered: registers, cache, RAM, disk, from fastest to biggest.
Pipelining overlaps instructions like an assembly line.
lessons.tip: Draw the diagrams yourself. CPU, buses and memory make much more sense when you sketch the boxes and arrows with your own hand.
lessons.task: Open your phone or computer settings and find the processor name, number of cores, RAM size and storage size. Write them down and label which one is the fastest and which one is the biggest.

quiz.q: What is the basic cycle the CPU repeats?
quiz.explain: The CPU fetches an instruction from memory, decodes what it means, then executes it, again and again.

quiz.q: Which memory is the fastest?
quiz.explain: Registers sit inside the CPU itself, so they are the fastest, but also the smallest.

quiz.q: Why do computers have cache memory?
options: To keep often-used data close to the CPU so it runs faster
quiz.explain: Cache keeps frequently used data close to the CPU, so it doesn't have to wait for slower RAM every time.

lessons.title: Microprocessors & Assembly Language
lessons.content:
A microprocessor is a whole CPU built on one tiny chip. Assembly language is the closest you can get to talking to that chip directly. Instead of writing something like total = a + b, you write tiny commands such as MOV, ADD and JMP that the chip understands almost word for word.

Why learn it? Every high level language like C or Python finally turns into these tiny instructions. Knowing assembly helps you understand what your code really costs, find nasty bugs, write code for tiny devices, and work in security, where people read assembly to understand viruses and cracks.

Here's how it works. You usually study a classic chip like the Intel 8086 or a modern one like ARM. You learn its registers (AX, BX and friends), how it reads and writes memory, and how flags tell you things like the last result was zero. You write small programs: add numbers, loop, compare, jump. You also learn interrupts, which let a keyboard press or a timer say hey CPU, stop and handle me now. Labs often use kits or simulators where you blink LEDs and read switches.

Real life example: think of giving directions to a very obedient but very simple rickshaw puller. With a smart friend you say take me to Dhanmondi. With the rickshaw puller you must say: go straight 200 meters, turn left, stop, turn right. Assembly is that second style. Each step is tiny, but nothing is hidden. Your microwave oven, washing machine and TV remote all have small microprocessors running programs like this.

After this course you will understand how software meets hardware, you will read simple assembly without fear, and you will be ready for embedded systems and IoT projects. It also makes compilers and operating systems much easier to understand later.
key_points: A microprocessor is a full CPU on a single chip.
Assembly uses tiny instructions like MOV, ADD and JMP.
Registers, flags and memory addresses are the main tools.
Interrupts let hardware get the CPU's attention right away.
lessons.tip: Use an emulator like emu8086 or an online assembly simulator. Watching registers change after every single instruction is the fastest way to learn.
lessons.task: Write the steps to add the numbers 1 to 5 using only these commands: put a value in a box, add a box to another box, subtract 1, and jump back if not zero. Use 2 boxes named A and B.

quiz.q: What is a microprocessor?
options: A CPU built on a single chip
quiz.explain: A microprocessor puts the whole CPU on one integrated circuit chip.

quiz.q: Which is an assembly-style instruction?
quiz.explain: ADD AX, BX adds two registers. It is a typical low level assembly instruction.

quiz.q: What does an interrupt do?
options: Makes the CPU pause and handle an urgent event
quiz.explain: An interrupt signals the CPU to pause its current work and run special code for an event like a key press.

lessons.title: Numerical Methods
lessons.content:
Some math problems are too hard to solve exactly with a formula. Numerical methods are clever tricks to get an answer that is close enough, using lots of small, simple calculations that a computer is great at.

Why does it matter? Weather forecasts, bridge designs, rocket paths, game physics, and even the way your phone calculator finds a square root all use numerical methods. In the real world, an answer correct to 6 decimal places is usually perfect.

Here's how it works. You learn how to find roots of equations, which means where a curve hits zero, using methods like bisection (keep cutting the range in half) and Newton-Raphson (follow the slope to jump closer). You learn interpolation, which means guessing the values between known points. You learn numerical integration, like the trapezoidal and Simpson's rules, which find areas by adding up small slices. You learn to solve many equations together, like Gauss elimination, and to solve differential equations step by step with Euler and Runge-Kutta. You also learn about errors, because every shortcut has a small mistake, and you must know how big it is.

Real life example: imagine finding the square root of 10 without a calculator. Guess 3. 3 times 3 is 9, too small. Try 3.2, that is 10.24, too big. Try 3.16, that is 9.98, close! Keep improving and you get closer and closer. That is exactly what a numerical method does, just super fast. Or think about measuring the area of an oddly shaped pond: cut it into thin strips, measure each, add them up.

After this course you can solve real engineering math with code and judge how accurate your answer is. It is a great base for machine learning, simulation and scientific computing.
key_points: Numerical methods find close-enough answers when exact formulas are hard.
Root finding: bisection and Newton-Raphson.
Integration by adding small slices: trapezoidal and Simpson's rules.
Always measure the error of your approximation.
lessons.tip: Code every method in a few lines of Python or C. Watching the answer get closer with every loop makes the math click.
lessons.task: Find the square root of 20 by guessing: start with 4, then improve your guess step by step until your guess times itself is within 0.1 of 20. Count how many tries it took.

quiz.q: What do numerical methods usually give us?
quiz.explain: Numerical methods produce approximations that can be made as accurate as we need.

quiz.q: Which method keeps cutting the range in half to find a root?
quiz.explain: The bisection method halves the interval each time, keeping the half where the curve crosses zero.

quiz.q: Trapezoidal and Simpson's rules are used for...
quiz.explain: Both rules estimate the area under a curve by adding up small slices.

lessons.title: Theory of Computation
lessons.content:
This course asks a big question: what can a computer do, and what can it never do, no matter how fast it gets? It studies imaginary simple machines to find the limits of computing.

Why learn it? It is the foundation behind programming languages, compilers, search patterns (regex) and even security. It also teaches you that some problems are impossible to solve and others are possible but way too slow, so you don't waste years trying.

Here's how it works. You start with finite automata, tiny machines with a few states that read input one letter at a time. They power regular expressions and things like checking if an email looks valid. Then pushdown automata, which add a stack and can check things like matching brackets, which is how compilers read code. Then the big one: the Turing machine, a simple model that can do anything any real computer can do. Then you learn about undecidable problems, like the halting problem: no program can always tell whether another program will finish or loop forever. Finally you meet P vs NP, the famous million-dollar question about easy-to-check versus easy-to-solve problems.

Real life example: a vending machine is a finite automaton. It has states like 0 taka, 5 taka, 10 taka. Each coin moves it to a new state, and when it reaches the right amount, it gives you a chips packet. It doesn't need memory of the past, just its current state. Or think of a sudoku: checking a filled one is fast, but solving a huge one can be crazy slow. That is the flavor of P vs NP.

After this course you can design small state machines, write and understand regular expressions, and know when a problem is impossible or just very hard. It prepares you for compiler design and advanced algorithms.
key_points: Finite automata are tiny state machines behind regex and vending machines.
Pushdown automata add a stack, useful for matching brackets and parsing.
Turing machines model everything a real computer can compute.
Some problems are undecidable, like the halting problem.
lessons.tip: Draw state diagrams with circles and arrows for every problem. Theory becomes a fun puzzle when you can see the machine.
lessons.task: Draw a state machine for a turnstile gate: states Locked and Unlocked, inputs Coin and Push. Show what happens for every input in every state.

quiz.q: A vending machine that changes state with each coin is an example of...
quiz.explain: It has a fixed set of states and moves between them based on input, which is exactly a finite automaton.

quiz.q: What does the halting problem show?
options: No program can always decide if another program will stop
quiz.explain: Turing proved no general program can decide for every program and input whether it will halt.

quiz.q: Which machine adds a stack to a finite automaton?
quiz.explain: A pushdown automaton is a finite automaton plus a stack, which lets it handle things like nested brackets.

lessons.title: Data Communication
lessons.content:
Data communication is about how bits, the 0s and 1s, travel from one device to another through wires, fiber or air. Before you build networks, you need to know how a single message actually gets carried.

Why learn it? Every phone call, bKash payment, YouTube video and WhatsApp message is data traveling somewhere. Mobile companies, ISPs and anyone building network hardware rely on these ideas. It is the physical base of the whole internet.

Here's how it works. You learn signals: analog (smooth waves) and digital (on and off). You learn bandwidth, which is how much data fits through per second, and noise, which messes signals up. You learn encoding and modulation, how 0s and 1s are turned into voltages, light pulses or radio waves (AM, FM, and more advanced kinds). You learn multiplexing, sharing one line among many users, like FDM and TDM. You learn transmission media: twisted pair, coaxial cable, fiber optics and wireless. And you learn error detection and correction, like parity and CRC, so the receiver can spot a broken message and ask for it again.

Real life example: imagine two friends using flashlights at night to talk across a field. Light on means 1, off means 0. They agree on speed so they don't get confused (that is a protocol and timing). If fog comes, some flashes get missed (that is noise). So they add an extra flash to check if the count is even (that is parity). Now think of the radio: many stations share the air, each on its own frequency. That is frequency division multiplexing.

After this course you will understand how data physically moves, why WiFi slows down far from the router, and why fiber is so fast. It leads straight into computer networks.
key_points: Data travels as signals, analog or digital.
Modulation turns bits into waves, light or voltage.
Multiplexing lets many users share one line.
Parity and CRC detect errors in received data.
lessons.tip: Connect every topic to a device you use: WiFi, mobile data, fiber broadband, FM radio. Real gadgets make the theory stick.
lessons.task: Write your name in binary using ASCII codes (search an ASCII table), then add a parity bit to each letter so the number of 1s is even.

quiz.q: What is multiplexing?
options: Sharing one channel among many signals
quiz.explain: Multiplexing combines many signals over a single medium, like many radio stations sharing the air.

quiz.q: Which medium carries data as light pulses?
quiz.explain: Fiber optic cables send data as pulses of light, which is why they are so fast.

quiz.q: What is a parity bit used for?
quiz.explain: A parity bit lets the receiver check whether a bit got flipped during transmission.

lessons.title: Operating Systems
lessons.content:
An operating system, or OS, is the manager program that runs your whole computer. Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS are all operating systems. Every other app sits on top of it and asks it for help.

Why learn it? Without an OS, every app would need to control the screen, memory and disk by itself. That would be chaos. The OS shares the computer fairly and safely between many programs. Knowing how it works helps you write faster apps, fix weird bugs and build servers that don't crash.

Here's how it works. You learn processes and threads: a running program and the little workers inside it. You learn CPU scheduling, how the OS decides who runs next, using ideas like first-come first-served, round robin and priorities. You learn memory management, how each program gets its own space with paging and virtual memory. You learn synchronization and deadlock, what happens when two programs fight over the same thing. And you learn file systems, how files and folders are stored on a disk.

Real life example: think of a busy school headmaster. Many teachers want the one projector, the hall and the playground. The headmaster makes a timetable (scheduling), gives each class its own room (memory), keeps a register of everything (file system) and stops two teachers from grabbing the projector at once (synchronization). If teacher A holds the projector and waits for the hall, while teacher B holds the hall and waits for the projector, nobody moves. That is a deadlock! On your phone, when you switch between YouTube and Messenger, Android is doing this juggling act.

After this course you will understand what happens behind every app, use Linux with confidence and handle threads in your own code. Next, it helps a lot with networks, databases and distributed systems.
key_points: The OS manages CPU, memory, files and devices for all programs.
Scheduling decides which process runs next.
Virtual memory and paging give each program its own space.
Deadlock happens when processes wait on each other forever.
lessons.tip: Install Linux in a virtual machine or use WSL and play with commands like ps, top and kill. Seeing processes live makes the chapters real.
lessons.task: Open Task Manager on Windows or Activity Monitor on Mac (or running apps on your phone). List 5 processes and note how much memory and CPU each one is using.

quiz.q: Which of these is an operating system?
quiz.explain: Android is an OS. The others are apps that run on top of an OS.

quiz.q: Round robin is a type of...
quiz.explain: Round robin gives each process a small time slice in turn, a classic CPU scheduling method.

quiz.q: Two processes each holding something the other needs, and both waiting forever, is called...
quiz.explain: That circular waiting is a deadlock, and OS designers work hard to prevent or detect it.

lessons.title: Database Management Systems
lessons.content:
A database is an organized place to store data so you can find, add and change it quickly. A DBMS, like MySQL, PostgreSQL or Oracle, is the software that manages that data safely for you.

Why learn it? Almost every app keeps data: users, orders, messages, marks. Daraz keeps products and orders, banks keep accounts, your university keeps results. Without a database, all that would be messy files that break easily. Database skills are among the most wanted skills in the software job market.

Here's how it works. You learn the relational model, where data lives in tables with rows and columns. You draw ER diagrams to plan which tables you need. You learn SQL, the language to ask questions like show me all students with GPA above 3.5. You learn normalization, which means splitting tables smartly so the same information isn't stored in five places. You learn indexing, which makes searches fast, and transactions with ACID rules, which make sure money transfers either fully happen or don't happen at all.

Real life example: think of a big school register. One table lists students with roll numbers. Another table lists subjects. A third table connects them with marks. If a student changes their phone number, you fix it in one place only. Now think of a bKash transfer: money must leave your account and arrive in your friend's account together. If the power goes out in the middle, the transaction rolls back so no money disappears. That is ACID at work.

After this course you can design tables for any app, write SQL queries, and keep data correct and fast. Next, you can explore NoSQL databases like MongoDB and big data systems.
key_points: A DBMS stores and manages data safely and quickly.
Relational databases use tables, and SQL to query them.
Normalization avoids storing the same data many times.
Transactions follow ACID so data stays correct.
lessons.tip: Install SQLite or use an online SQL playground and practice queries daily. SQL is learned by typing, not by reading.
lessons.task: Design tables on paper for a small library: books, members and borrowings. Decide the columns for each and which column links them together.

quiz.q: What is SQL used for?
options: Asking and changing data in a database
quiz.explain: SQL is the standard language for querying and updating relational databases.

quiz.q: Why do we normalize tables?
options: To avoid repeating the same data in many places
quiz.explain: Normalization removes duplicate data, so updates happen in one place and data stays consistent.

quiz.q: A money transfer that must fully happen or not happen at all relies on...
quiz.explain: Transactions with ACID properties guarantee all-or-nothing behavior, even if something fails midway.

lessons.title: Computer Networks
lessons.content:
Computer networks are about how computers connect and talk to each other, from two laptops on the same WiFi to billions of devices across the internet.

Why learn it? Every app today talks to a server somewhere. Messenger, online games, Pathao, online classes, all need networks. Network engineers, backend developers, cloud engineers and security experts all need this knowledge daily.

Here's how it works. You learn the layered model: TCP/IP (and the 7-layer OSI model). Each layer has one job, like a team passing a parcel along. The application layer has protocols like HTTP for websites and DNS for turning names like google.com into numbers. The transport layer has TCP, which is reliable and makes sure nothing is lost, and UDP, which is fast but doesn't check, great for live video and games. The network layer has IP addresses and routers that find paths. The link layer handles local delivery with things like Ethernet and WiFi. You also learn subnetting, routing algorithms and congestion control.

Real life example: sending a parcel with a courier like Sundarban or Pathao. You write the receiver's address (IP address). The courier breaks a big shipment into boxes (packets). Each box may take a different route through different hubs (routers) but all reach the same place. The receiver counts the boxes and asks for missing ones again (TCP). And when you type facebook.com, DNS is like the phone book that finds Facebook's actual number before your phone can call it.

After this course you will understand what happens when you open a website, set up a small network, and debug problems like no internet. Next, network security and distributed systems build directly on this.
key_points: Networks are built in layers, each with one job.
IP addresses identify devices; routers find paths.
TCP is reliable, UDP is fast but unchecked.
DNS turns names like google.com into IP addresses.
lessons.tip: Use tools like ping, tracert/traceroute and Wireshark. Watching real packets fly makes protocols far easier to remember.
lessons.task: Open a command prompt or terminal and run: ping google.com. Note the IP address and the time in milliseconds. Then try a website from another country and compare.

quiz.q: What does DNS do?
options: Turns domain names into IP addresses
quiz.explain: DNS works like a phone book, translating names like google.com into IP addresses.

quiz.q: Which protocol makes sure no data is lost?
quiz.explain: TCP numbers the data, confirms delivery and resends missing pieces.

quiz.q: What device finds paths and forwards packets between networks?
quiz.explain: Routers read the destination address and forward packets toward it.

lessons.title: Software Engineering
lessons.content:
Writing a small program alone is easy. Building big software with a team, on time, that keeps working for years is hard. Software engineering is the art of doing that properly.

Why learn it? Most software projects fail not because people can't code, but because of bad planning, unclear requirements and messy teamwork. Companies want engineers who can plan, write clean code, test it and work well in a team. This course teaches the real job, not just the coding part.

Here's how it works. You learn the software development life cycle: requirements (what to build), design, coding, testing, deployment and maintenance. You learn process models: the old waterfall model, where you finish each step before the next, and Agile methods like Scrum, where you build in small 2-week sprints and improve constantly. You learn UML diagrams to show design, version control with Git, different kinds of testing, estimating time and cost, and managing risk.

Real life example: building a house. You don't just start putting bricks. First you ask the family what they need: how many rooms, a kitchen, a balcony (requirements). The architect draws a plan (design). Workers build (coding). An engineer checks for cracks (testing). The family moves in (deployment), and later you fix leaks or add a floor (maintenance). Apps like bKash or Pathao follow the same steps, just with code, and they release updates every few weeks using Agile.

After this course you can work in a real software team, plan a project, use Git and write tests. Your final year project and every job after will use these skills every single day.
key_points: SDLC: requirements, design, coding, testing, deployment, maintenance.
Waterfall goes step by step; Agile builds in small sprints.
Git lets a team work on the same code safely.
Testing catches bugs before users do.
lessons.tip: Treat every class project like a real product: write a short requirements list, use Git from day one and write at least a few tests.
lessons.task: Pick an app you use daily. Write 5 requirements for it in the form: As a user, I want to ... so that ... . This is called a user story.

quiz.q: Which step comes first in the software life cycle?
quiz.explain: You must first know what to build, so gathering requirements comes first.

quiz.q: Building software in short sprints and improving often is called...
quiz.explain: Agile methods like Scrum deliver small working pieces frequently and adapt to feedback.

quiz.q: What is Git mainly used for?
options: Version control and team collaboration on code
quiz.explain: Git tracks every change in code and lets many people work together without overwriting each other.

lessons.title: Compiler Design
lessons.content:
A compiler is a translator. It takes the code you write in a language like C or Java and turns it into instructions the machine can run. This course shows how to build that translator step by step.

Why learn it? Every time you hit run, a compiler or interpreter is working hard. Learning how it works makes you understand error messages, write faster code and even create your own small language. The same ideas are used in code editors, formatters, SQL engines and tools like Flutter and TypeScript.

Here's how it works. The compiler works in phases. Lexical analysis reads your code and splits it into tokens, like words in a sentence. Syntax analysis (parsing) checks that the tokens follow the grammar rules and builds a tree. Semantic analysis checks the meaning, like you can't add a number to a list. Then the compiler creates intermediate code, optimizes it to make it faster or smaller, and finally generates machine code. A symbol table keeps track of all variable names along the way.

Real life example: think of translating a Bangla story into English. First you split the sentences into words (lexical). Then you check the grammar is right (syntax). Then you check it makes sense, because the rice ate the boy is grammatically fine but meaningless (semantic). Then you write the English version and polish it to sound natural (optimization and code generation). Google Translate does a similar journey for human languages.

After this course you can build a small calculator language or interpreter, read compiler errors like a pro and understand how languages really work. It connects theory of computation with real programming.
key_points: A compiler translates source code into machine code.
Phases: lexical, syntax, semantic analysis, then code generation.
Optimization makes the output faster or smaller.
The symbol table tracks all names in the program.
lessons.tip: Build a tiny project: a calculator that reads text like 2 + 3 * 4 and gives the right answer. It teaches you lexing and parsing better than any book.
lessons.task: Take the line: total = price * 2 + 10; and split it into tokens on paper. Label each one as a name, number, operator or symbol.

quiz.q: Which phase splits code into tokens?
quiz.explain: Lexical analysis reads characters and groups them into tokens such as names, numbers and operators.

quiz.q: Checking that code follows grammar rules is called...
quiz.explain: The parser checks grammar and builds a parse tree from the tokens.

quiz.q: What does code optimization do?
options: Makes the output code faster or smaller
quiz.explain: Optimization improves the generated code so it runs faster or uses less memory, without changing what it does.

lessons.title: System Analysis & Design
lessons.content:
Before building any software for a business, someone has to understand how that business works and what it really needs. System analysis is studying the problem. System design is planning the solution.

Why learn it? Many projects build the wrong thing, perfectly. A system analyst talks to people, finds the real problems and turns them into a clear plan that developers can build. This role sits between business people and programmers, and it is a great career path.

Here's how it works. You learn to gather requirements through interviews, surveys and observing people at work. You check feasibility: is it possible technically, affordable and worth it? You draw models: data flow diagrams (DFD) to show how information moves, ER diagrams for data, use case diagrams for who does what, and flowcharts. Then you design inputs, outputs, screens, reports and databases. Finally you plan testing, training users and switching from the old system to the new one.

Real life example: imagine a pharmacy in your area that still uses a paper khata. The analyst visits, watches how medicines are sold, how stock is counted and why they often run out of popular medicines. She finds the real problem: nobody knows stock levels. So the design includes a simple app with a sales screen, a stock report and an alert when stock is low. The developers now know exactly what to build, and the owner gets what he actually needs.

After this course you can study any organization, find its pain points and design a computer system that fits. It is perfect preparation for your final year project and for roles like business analyst or product manager.
key_points: Analysis studies the problem; design plans the solution.
Gather requirements by interviews, surveys and observation.
Feasibility checks if a system is possible, affordable and worth it.
DFDs, ER diagrams and use cases model the system.
lessons.tip: Practice on real places: a shop, a clinic, your department office. Talking to real users teaches more than any textbook example.
lessons.task: Pick a small shop near you. Write down 3 problems it faces with its current way of working, and for each, one feature a simple app could add to fix it.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of system analysis?
options: Understanding the problem and real needs
quiz.explain: Analysis focuses on understanding the current situation and what users truly need.

quiz.q: A diagram showing how information moves through a system is a...
quiz.explain: A DFD shows the flow of data between processes, data stores and outside entities.

quiz.q: A feasibility study checks whether a system is...
quiz.explain: Feasibility looks at technical, economic and practical sides before committing to a project.

lessons.title: Artificial Intelligence
lessons.content:
Artificial Intelligence, or AI, is about making computers do things that look smart. Things like playing chess, finding the shortest road, understanding a question or deciding what to do next. The computer is not alive and does not really think. It follows clever methods that make it act as if it does.

Why learn it? Because AI is everywhere now. Google Maps picks your route, games have enemies that chase you, and chatbots answer your questions. This course gives you the classic tools that all of that is built on.

Here's how it works. First you learn about agents: a program that looks at its world, then picks an action. Then you learn search: trying out possible moves like a maze runner, using methods such as BFS, DFS and A*, which uses a smart guess called a heuristic to go faster. Then game playing with minimax, where the computer imagines your best move before choosing its own. You also learn how to store facts and rules (knowledge representation and logic) and how to make decisions when you are not sure, using probability.

Real life example: imagine you are lost in Old Dhaka and want to reach Lalbagh Fort. You could try every lane one by one, which takes forever. Or you could always walk toward the fort's direction, which is a heuristic. That is exactly what A* search does on a map. And when you play Ludo against your phone, the phone is quietly checking which move helps it most and hurts you most. That is minimax.

After this course you can make a program that solves puzzles, finds paths and plays simple games well. Next step: Machine Learning, where the computer learns its own rules from data.
key_points: AI makes computers act smart by following clever methods.
Search methods like BFS, DFS and A* explore possible moves to find a goal.
A heuristic is a smart guess that makes search faster.
Minimax helps a computer pick the best move in a two-player game.
lessons.tip: Draw the search on paper. A tiny maze with 6 boxes and arrows will teach you BFS and DFS faster than any slide.
lessons.task: Draw a 4 by 4 grid maze on paper with a start and a goal. Find a path by always trying the box closest to the goal first. Count how many boxes you checked.

quiz.q: What does a heuristic do in search?
options: It gives a smart guess to reach the goal faster
quiz.explain: A heuristic is an estimate, like how far the goal is, so the search tries promising paths first.

quiz.q: Which method helps a computer choose moves in tic-tac-toe or chess?
quiz.explain: Minimax imagines the opponent's best reply and picks the move that is safest for the computer.

quiz.q: In AI, an agent is...
options: A program that senses its world and picks actions
quiz.explain: An agent looks at its environment and decides what action to take.

lessons.title: Computer Graphics
lessons.content:
Computer Graphics is about how a computer draws pictures. Every game, cartoon, phone screen and button you see was drawn by math. This course teaches you that math and the tricks behind it.

Why learn it? Games like PUBG or FIFA, animated movies, 3D house designs, and even the smooth swipe on your phone all need graphics. If you want to make games, animations or visual apps, this is your home course.

Here's how it works. A screen is a big grid of tiny dots called pixels. To draw a line, the computer must decide which pixels to color, using methods like Bresenham's line algorithm. Shapes are moved, turned and resized using transformations: translation, rotation and scaling, which are done with matrices. For 3D, objects are made of tiny triangles. A camera view and projection squash the 3D world onto your flat screen. Then lighting and shading decide how bright each part looks, and textures paint images onto the surfaces.

Real life example: think of a cricket game on your phone. The ball is a 3D sphere made of many little triangles. When it flies, the game uses translation to move it and rotation to spin it, sixty times every second. The stadium lights make one side of the ball bright and the other side dark. That is shading. The grass pattern on the field is a texture, just a picture wrapped onto the ground.

After this course you understand how pixels, shapes, cameras and light come together on a screen. You can write a small drawing program, or move on to game engines like Unity, or to Digital Image Processing.
key_points: A screen is a grid of pixels, and graphics decides each pixel's color.
Translation, rotation and scaling move shapes, using matrices.
3D objects are built from triangles and projected onto a 2D screen.
Lighting, shading and textures make things look real.
lessons.tip: Graphics is math you can see. Whenever a formula feels dry, draw it on graph paper and watch the shape move.
lessons.task: On graph paper draw a small square. Now move it 3 boxes right (translation), then double its size (scaling). Write the new corner points each time.

quiz.q: What is a pixel?
options: A tiny dot on the screen
quiz.explain: A screen is made of many tiny colored dots called pixels.

quiz.q: Moving a shape from one place to another without turning it is called...
quiz.explain: Translation just shifts a shape. Rotation turns it and scaling resizes it.

quiz.q: 3D objects in games are usually built from...
quiz.explain: Graphics cards are very fast at drawing triangles, so 3D models are made of many small triangles.

lessons.title: Web Engineering
lessons.content:
Web Engineering is about building websites and web apps the right way. Not just one pretty page, but real sites like Daraz or Prothom Alo that many people use at the same time.

Why learn it? Almost every business needs a website. Shops, schools, banks and news sites all live on the web. Web skills are also one of the fastest ways to get freelance work or a job.

Here's how it works. When you type a web address, your browser sends a request to a server using HTTP. The server sends back a page. That page is built from three things: HTML for the structure (headings, text, buttons), CSS for the looks (colors, sizes, layout), and JavaScript for the actions (what happens when you click). That part is the frontend. The backend is the server side, written in languages like PHP, Python, Node.js or Java. It talks to a database, checks logins and handles orders. You also learn about APIs, sessions and cookies, security and how to make sites fast and mobile friendly.

Real life example: think of a restaurant. The menu card and the nice table are the frontend, what you see. The kitchen is the backend, where the real work happens. The waiter is HTTP, carrying your order to the kitchen and bringing food back. The fridge with all the ingredients is the database. When you order a phone on Daraz, the same thing happens: the page takes your order, the server checks stock in the database, and sends back "Order placed".

After this course you can build a full website with a login, a database and a nice look. Next, try a framework like React or Laravel and build your own project.
key_points: The browser asks the server for pages using HTTP.
HTML gives structure, CSS gives style, JavaScript gives action.
The frontend is what users see; the backend works on the server with the database.
Real websites must be fast, secure and work on phones.
lessons.tip: Build while you learn. After every class, add one small thing to your own personal website.
lessons.task: On any website, right-click and choose "View page source" (on a computer) or just look closely at a page. List 3 things you think are HTML, 3 that are CSS, and 1 that needs JavaScript.

quiz.q: Which language mainly controls how a web page looks, like colors and layout?
quiz.explain: CSS is for style. HTML is for structure and JavaScript is for behavior.

quiz.q: In the restaurant example, the backend is like the...
quiz.explain: The kitchen does the real work out of sight, just like the backend server.

quiz.q: What does the browser use to ask a server for a page?
quiz.explain: HTTP (or HTTPS) is the language browsers and servers use to talk.

lessons.title: Mobile Application Development
lessons.content:
Mobile Application Development is about building apps for phones, like bKash, Pathao or a simple calculator. You learn how to make apps that run on Android and iPhone.

Why learn it? People spend hours on their phones every day. Banks, shops, ride sharing and games all want apps. A good app idea, built well, can reach millions of people from one small team.

Here's how it works. Android apps are usually written in Kotlin or Java, and iPhone apps in Swift. You can also use cross-platform tools like Flutter or React Native, where one code works on both. An app is made of screens. Each screen has widgets or views: buttons, text, images, lists. You learn the app lifecycle, which is what happens when the app opens, goes to the background or closes. You learn to save data on the phone, call online APIs, use phone features like the camera and GPS, and ask the user for permission before using them. Phones have small screens, weak batteries and slow internet sometimes, so apps must be light and smart.

Real life example: open Pathao. The map screen uses GPS to find you. When you tap "Book", the app sends a request to Pathao's server through an API. The server finds a nearby rider and sends back their name and location. If you get a phone call in the middle, the app goes to the background and must not lose your ride. That is the lifecycle in action. And it asked for location permission the very first time. That is privacy done right.

After this course you can build and publish your own app. Start small: a to-do list or an expense tracker, then put it on the Play Store.
key_points: Android uses Kotlin or Java, iPhone uses Swift, and Flutter works for both.
Apps are made of screens with widgets like buttons, text and lists.
The lifecycle handles what happens when an app opens, pauses or closes.
Apps must ask permission for things like the camera and location.
lessons.tip: Copy apps you love. Rebuild one screen of a famous app by yourself, and you will learn more than from ten tutorials.
lessons.task: Pick any app on your phone. Draw its main screen on paper and label each part: button, text, image, list. Then write what happens when you tap each button.

quiz.q: Which tool lets you write one code for both Android and iPhone?
quiz.explain: Flutter (and React Native) are cross-platform, so one codebase runs on both.

quiz.q: What is the app lifecycle about?
options: How long a phone battery lasts
What happens when an app opens, goes to background or closes
quiz.explain: The lifecycle is the set of stages an app goes through while running.

quiz.q: Before using the camera or location, a good app should...
quiz.explain: Phones protect privacy, so apps must ask the user before using sensitive features.

lessons.title: Human Computer Interaction
lessons.content:
Human Computer Interaction, or HCI, is about how people and computers work together. It asks one big question: is this app or machine easy and pleasant for a real person to use?

Why learn it? A powerful app that nobody understands is a failure. If your grandmother cannot send money on an app, the app is the problem, not your grandmother. HCI teaches you to design for real people.

Here's how it works. You learn usability: is it easy to learn, quick to use, and hard to make mistakes? You learn design rules, like Nielsen's heuristics: show what is happening, use words people know, let people undo, keep things consistent. You learn user research: talk to users, watch them, and make personas, which are imaginary but realistic users. You make prototypes, from paper sketches to clickable screens, and test them with real people. You also learn accessibility, so people with weak eyes, color blindness or other needs can use your product too.

Real life example: think of a lift (elevator). If the "open door" and "close door" buttons look almost the same, people press the wrong one and doors close on someone. That is bad HCI. Now think of a bKash app showing "Are you sure you want to send 500 taka to this number?" before the money goes. That pause saves people from mistakes. Good HCI. Even a big, clear "Back" button helps someone who is new to smartphones.

After this course you will look at every app and machine with new eyes. You can test designs with users and fix what confuses them. Next, try UI/UX design tools like Figma.
key_points: HCI is about making technology easy and pleasant for real people.
Good design is easy to learn, fast to use and prevents mistakes.
Talk to users, make prototypes, and test with real people.
Accessibility means everyone, including people with disabilities, can use it.
lessons.tip: You are not your user. Always test with someone else, like a parent or a friend, and just watch quietly.
lessons.task: Give your phone to a family member and ask them to do one small task in an app, like set an alarm. Do not help. Write down every place they got stuck.

quiz.q: If users keep pressing the wrong button, what does HCI say?
quiz.explain: In HCI, repeated user mistakes point to a design problem, not a user problem.

quiz.q: A persona is...
options: A realistic imaginary user used in design
quiz.explain: Personas help designers remember who they are building for.

quiz.q: Making an app usable for people with weak eyesight is called...
quiz.explain: Accessibility means designing so people with different abilities can use the product.

lessons.title: Embedded Systems
lessons.content:
An Embedded System is a small computer hidden inside another machine, doing one job. Your microwave, washing machine, TV remote, digital weighing scale and car all have tiny computers inside them.

Why learn it? There are far more embedded computers in the world than laptops and phones put together. Robots, smart devices, medical machines and cars all need people who can program small chips that touch the real world.

Here's how it works. The brain is usually a microcontroller, a tiny chip with a processor, a little memory and input/output pins, all in one. Popular ones are Arduino (AVR) and ARM chips like STM32 or ESP32. Sensors give input: temperature, light, distance, a button press. Actuators give output: a motor, an LED, a buzzer. You write code, often in C, that reads sensors and controls actuators in a loop. Many systems are real-time, meaning they must answer within a fixed time, like an airbag. You also learn interrupts, timers, saving power, and ways chips talk to each other like UART, I2C and SPI.

Real life example: think of an automatic water pump controller on a building's roof tank, very common in Dhaka. A sensor checks the water level. When the tank is almost empty, the little chip turns the motor on. When it is full, it turns the motor off. No human needed. The same idea runs a rice cooker that switches to "warm" when the rice is done.

After this course you can build small smart gadgets with an Arduino, sensors and motors. Next step: Internet of Things, where these little gadgets talk over the internet.
key_points: An embedded system is a small computer inside a machine, doing one job.
A microcontroller has a processor, memory and pins on one chip.
Sensors give input; actuators like motors and LEDs give output.
Real-time systems must respond within a strict time limit.
lessons.tip: Buy a cheap Arduino kit. Blinking one LED with your own code feels like magic and keeps you motivated.
lessons.task: Walk around your home and list 5 machines that have a tiny computer inside. For each one, write one sensor (input) and one actuator (output) it might have.

quiz.q: Which of these is an embedded system?
quiz.explain: A microwave has a small computer inside that controls time and power.

quiz.q: In an embedded system, a motor or buzzer is an...
quiz.explain: Actuators produce action or output. Sensors read input from the world.

quiz.q: A real-time system must...
quiz.explain: For things like airbags or brakes, a late answer is a wrong answer.

lessons.title: Machine Learning
lessons.content:
Machine Learning, or ML, is about teaching computers by showing examples instead of writing every rule. You show a computer thousands of cat and dog photos, and it learns by itself how to tell them apart.

Why learn it? ML is behind Facebook's friend suggestions, YouTube's next video, spam filters in Gmail, face unlock on your phone and fraud checks in banks. It is one of the most wanted skills in tech today.

Here's how it works. You start with data: lots of examples. In supervised learning every example has the right answer (a label), like "this email is spam". The computer builds a model that maps input to answer. Common models are linear regression (predict a number), logistic regression and decision trees (pick a class), k-nearest neighbors, SVM and simple neural networks. In unsupervised learning there are no labels, and the computer finds groups by itself, like k-means clustering. You split data into training and testing parts, so you can check if the model really learned or just memorized. Memorizing is called overfitting, and it is the classic trap.

Real life example: imagine guessing the price of a flat in Dhaka. You collect 1000 flats: size, area, floor, and their prices. The model learns the pattern, like "bigger flats in Gulshan cost more". Now give it a new flat and it predicts a price. That is regression. And when your phone's keyboard guesses your next word in Banglish, it learned that from tons of typed text.

After this course you can train simple models in Python with tools like scikit-learn, and judge if they are good. Next step: Deep Learning.
key_points: ML learns patterns from examples instead of hand-written rules.
Supervised learning uses labeled data; unsupervised finds groups by itself.
Always test on data the model has never seen.
Overfitting means the model memorized instead of learning.
lessons.tip: Spend most of your time understanding the data. A simple model on clean data beats a fancy model on messy data.
lessons.task: Write down the last 7 days: hours you slept and how fresh you felt (1 to 5). Look for a pattern. Can you predict tomorrow's freshness from sleep? That is a tiny ML model in your head.

quiz.q: In supervised learning, the training data has...
quiz.explain: Supervised learning learns from examples where the right answer is already given.

quiz.q: A model that does great on training data but badly on new data is...
quiz.explain: Overfitting means it memorized the training examples instead of learning the general pattern.

quiz.q: Predicting a flat's price (a number) is an example of...
quiz.explain: Regression predicts a number. Classification predicts a category.

lessons.title: Computer Security & Cryptography
lessons.content:
Computer Security is about keeping data and systems safe from bad people. Cryptography is the art of secret codes, turning a message into gibberish that only the right person can read.

Why learn it? Every day hackers try to steal passwords, money and private photos. Banks, bKash, hospitals and governments need security experts. Even you need it to stay safe online.

Here's how it works. Security has three big goals, called CIA: Confidentiality (only the right people can see it), Integrity (nobody changes it secretly) and Availability (it works when needed). In cryptography you learn symmetric encryption, where one key locks and unlocks, like AES. Then public-key encryption, like RSA, where you have a public lock anyone can use and a private key only you keep. Hash functions, like SHA-256, turn data into a fingerprint, which is how websites store passwords safely. Digital signatures prove who sent something. You also learn common attacks: phishing, malware, SQL injection, denial of service, and how to defend against them with firewalls, updates and good habits.

Real life example: someone calls you saying "I'm from bKash, tell me your OTP so we can fix your account." That is phishing, a trick, not hacking with code. Security says: never share OTP or PIN. And the little lock icon next to a website address means HTTPS, where your browser and the site use public-key cryptography to agree on a secret key, so nobody in the middle can read your data.

After this course you understand how attacks work and how to protect systems. Next, try ethical hacking practice sites or a network security course.
key_points: Security goals are CIA: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability.
Symmetric encryption uses one key; public-key uses a public and private key pair.
Hashes are fingerprints of data, used to store passwords safely.
Many attacks trick humans, like phishing, not just machines.
lessons.tip: Think like an attacker. For any system you build, ask "How would I break this?" before someone else does.
lessons.task: Make a simple Caesar cipher: shift each letter 3 forward (A becomes D). Encrypt your name, give it to a friend with the rule, and let them decrypt it.

quiz.q: In public-key cryptography, which key must you keep secret?
quiz.explain: The public key can be shared with everyone. The private key must stay only with you.

quiz.q: Someone calls pretending to be from your bank and asks for your OTP. This is...
quiz.explain: Phishing tricks people into giving away secrets by pretending to be someone trusted.

quiz.q: What is a hash mainly used for?
options: Making a fingerprint of data, like for storing passwords
quiz.explain: A hash turns data into a fixed fingerprint. Websites store password hashes, not the passwords.

lessons.title: Distributed Systems
lessons.content:
A Distributed System is many computers working together so they look like one big system. Google, Facebook and YouTube are not one computer. They are thousands of computers in many countries, acting as one.

Why learn it? One computer cannot handle millions of users, and if it breaks, everything stops. Spreading the work across many machines makes systems faster, bigger and harder to kill. Almost every big app today is distributed.

Here's how it works. Computers talk by sending messages over a network. But networks are slow and can fail, and machines can crash anytime. So you learn replication: keeping copies of data on many machines, so if one dies, another has it. Consistency: making sure all copies agree. Consensus algorithms like Paxos and Raft help machines vote and agree, even when some fail. You learn about clocks, because each computer's time is slightly different. The CAP theorem says that when the network breaks, you must choose between always answering and always being perfectly consistent. You also learn load balancing, which spreads users across servers.

Real life example: think of a big cricket match on Toffee or a streaming site. Millions watch at once. One server would melt. So the video is copied to many servers in many cities, and a load balancer sends you to the nearest, least busy one. If a Dhaka server dies, you quietly get moved to another. You may not even notice. That is a distributed system doing its job.

After this course you understand how giant apps stay up. Next, explore Cloud Computing and tools like Kubernetes.
key_points: Many computers work together and look like one system.
Replication keeps copies of data so a failure does not lose it.
Consensus algorithms like Raft help machines agree.
The CAP theorem: during network failures you trade consistency against availability.
lessons.tip: In distributed systems, always ask "What if this message is lost or this machine dies right now?" That one question finds most bugs.
lessons.task: With 3 friends, each write a number on paper without talking. Now agree on one number by only passing notes. Notice how slow and tricky agreement is. That is consensus.

quiz.q: Why keep copies of data on many machines?
options: So data survives when a machine fails
quiz.explain: Replication makes the system survive failures.

quiz.q: Raft and Paxos are used for...
options: Helping machines agree on a value
quiz.explain: They are consensus algorithms that let many machines agree even if some fail.

quiz.q: A load balancer...
quiz.explain: It sends each request to a server that can handle it, so no one server is overloaded.

lessons.title: Digital Image Processing
lessons.content:
Digital Image Processing is about changing and understanding pictures with a computer. Brightening a dark photo, removing noise, finding edges, or cutting out a background are all image processing.

Why learn it? Every camera app, Instagram filter, medical X-ray tool, satellite map and number plate reader uses it. It is also the base for Computer Vision and AI that sees.

Here's how it works. A digital image is just a grid of numbers. In a gray image each pixel is a number from 0 (black) to 255 (white). A color image has three numbers per pixel: red, green and blue. You learn point operations, like adding to every pixel to make the image brighter. A histogram shows how many pixels are dark or bright, and histogram equalization fixes poor contrast. Filtering slides a small window, called a kernel, over the image: an average filter blurs and removes noise, edge detectors like Sobel find sharp changes. You also learn the Fourier transform (seeing an image as waves), segmentation (splitting objects), and compression like JPEG, which throws away details your eyes won't miss.

Real life example: take a photo at night at a wedding. It is dark and grainy. The phone brightens it (point operation), smooths the grain (filtering) and sharpens faces (edge enhancement). When you send it on Messenger, it gets compressed so it travels fast. And on a highway, a camera reads car number plates by finding edges and shapes of letters. All image processing.

After this course you can write code, for example with Python and OpenCV, to clean, edit and analyze pictures. Next step: Computer Vision.
key_points: An image is a grid of numbers; color images have red, green and blue values.
Histograms show brightness; equalization improves contrast.
Filters slide a kernel over the image to blur, sharpen or find edges.
JPEG compression removes details our eyes barely notice.
lessons.tip: Use OpenCV in Python and see results instantly. Seeing the output picture makes each formula click.
lessons.task: Open any photo editor on your phone. Change brightness, then contrast, then blur. For each one, write in one line what you think happens to the pixel numbers.

quiz.q: In an 8-bit gray image, a pixel value of 0 means...
quiz.explain: 0 is black and 255 is white in a usual 8-bit grayscale image.

quiz.q: An average (mean) filter is mainly used to...
quiz.explain: Averaging nearby pixels smooths out random noise, but also blurs details.

quiz.q: Which operation helps find the borders of objects?
quiz.explain: Edge detectors like Sobel find places where brightness changes sharply, which are object borders.

lessons.title: Simulation & Modeling
lessons.content:
Simulation and Modeling is about building a copy of a real system inside the computer, then playing with it to see what happens. You can test ideas without spending real money or risking real lives.

Why learn it? Pilots train in flight simulators. Engineers test bridges before building them. Shops decide how many cashiers they need. Governments plan roads and hospitals. All of them simulate first.

Here's how it works. First you make a model: a simple description of the system with only the important parts. Then you choose a type of simulation. Discrete-event simulation jumps from event to event, like "customer arrives", "service done". Continuous simulation changes smoothly over time, like water filling a tank. Monte Carlo simulation uses random numbers again and again to estimate answers. You learn random number generators and probability distributions, like Poisson for arrivals. Queuing theory studies lines and waiting times. Finally you validate: does the model behave like the real world? If not, fix it.

Real life example: think of a busy Agora or Shwapno supermarket on a Friday evening. How many cash counters should be open? Too few, and people get angry in long lines. Too many, and staff sit idle. Instead of guessing, you simulate: customers arrive randomly, each takes 2 to 5 minutes to pay. Run it 1000 times in the computer with 3, 4 and 5 counters. Now you know the best number. The same idea helps plan traffic signals at a busy crossing like Farmgate.

After this course you can model real problems and test "what if" questions safely. Try tools like Python with SimPy, or even a spreadsheet.
key_points: A model is a simplified copy of a real system.
Simulation lets you test "what if" ideas safely and cheaply.
Discrete-event, continuous and Monte Carlo are main types of simulation.
Always check that the model matches the real world.
lessons.tip: Start with the simplest model that could work. Add details only when the results look wrong.
lessons.task: Roll a dice 20 times and write each number. Pretend each number is how many minutes a customer takes at a shop. Add them up to estimate how long one cashier needs for 20 customers.

quiz.q: Why do companies simulate before doing things in real life?
options: To test ideas safely and cheaply
quiz.explain: Simulation saves money and risk by testing ideas in a computer first.

quiz.q: A simulation that uses random numbers many times to estimate a result is called...
quiz.explain: Monte Carlo simulation repeats random trials to estimate an answer.

quiz.q: Queuing theory is mostly about...
quiz.explain: Queuing theory studies how lines form and how long people wait.

lessons.title: Professional Ethics & Cyber Law
lessons.content:
Professional Ethics is about doing the right thing as a computer engineer. Cyber Law is the set of rules about computers, the internet and data, and what happens if you break them.

Why learn it? Your code can touch millions of lives. A bug in a hospital system can hurt patients. A careless app can leak people's private photos. Engineers must be skilled and also honest and responsible. And breaking cyber laws can mean fines or jail.

Here's how it works. You learn codes of ethics, like those of ACM and IEEE: be honest, avoid harm, respect privacy, give credit to others' work, and do not do work you are not able to do well. You learn about intellectual property: copyright, patents, software licenses like GPL and MIT, and why copying cracked software or code without permission is wrong. You learn privacy and data protection: collect only what you need and keep it safe. You study cyber crimes like hacking, online fraud, harassment and spreading fake news. In Bangladesh, laws like the ICT Act and later digital and cyber security laws cover these things, and other countries have their own, like the EU's GDPR for data privacy.

Real life example: imagine you build an app for a local shop, and you secretly see all customers' phone numbers. Selling that list to an ad company might make quick money, but it is a big ethical failure and may be illegal. Another one: you copy a friend's project code for your assignment. That is plagiarism. Small choices like these build your reputation for life.

After this course you can spot ethical problems early and know the legal basics of working in tech.
key_points: Engineers must be honest, avoid harm and respect privacy.
Copyright, patents and licenses protect people's work.
Collect only the data you need and protect it well.
Cyber laws punish hacking, fraud and online harassment.
lessons.tip: When unsure, ask: "Would I be okay if this decision appeared on the front page of a newspaper?" If not, don't do it.
lessons.task: Open the privacy settings of one app you use. Write down what data it collects (location, contacts, photos). Decide if each one is really needed.

quiz.q: Copying someone's code and submitting it as yours is...
quiz.explain: Using others' work without credit and calling it yours is plagiarism.

quiz.q: A good rule for user data is...
options: Collect only what you need and protect it
quiz.explain: Collect the minimum data and keep it safe. That protects users and you.

quiz.q: Which one protects an original software or book from being copied?
quiz.explain: Copyright gives creators legal rights over their original work.

lessons.title: Final Year Project / Thesis
lessons.content:
The Final Year Project or Thesis is your big solo or team mission at the end of BSc. Instead of exams on someone else's ideas, you pick a problem, solve it, build something, and present it.

Why do it? It shows you can use everything you learned in four years. It goes on your CV, it gives you a story to tell in job interviews, and for research lovers, it can become your first published paper. Many startups began as final year projects.

Here's how it works. A project usually means building a working system, like an app or a device. A thesis usually means research: asking a new question and answering it with experiments. Both follow similar steps. Pick a topic you care about and a supervisor who guides you. Do a literature review, which means reading what others have already done. Write a proposal: the problem, your plan and your timeline. Then build or experiment, step by step, and keep notes. Test and measure results honestly. Finally, write the report, with chapters like introduction, related work, method, results and conclusion, and defend it in front of teachers.

Real life example: say you notice farmers in your village can't tell which disease their rice plants have. Your project: a mobile app that takes a photo of a leaf and uses machine learning to guess the disease. You read papers about plant disease detection, collect leaf photos, train a model, build the app, test it with real farmers, and write about how accurate it was. That is a full, meaningful final year project.

After this, you are not just a student. You are someone who has built or discovered something real.
key_points: A project builds a working system; a thesis answers a research question.
Read related work first, so you don't repeat what exists.
Make a proposal with a clear problem, plan and timeline.
Report results honestly, even when they are not perfect.
lessons.tip: Pick a problem you truly care about. You will live with it for many months, and passion keeps you going when bugs pile up.
lessons.task: Write 3 problems you have seen around you that tech could help with. For each one, write one sentence about what you might build.

quiz.q: What is a literature review?
options: Studying what others have already done on your topic
quiz.explain: A literature review shows what exists, so your work adds something new.

quiz.q: Which is usually more about a research question and experiments?
quiz.explain: A thesis focuses on research; a project focuses more on building a system.

quiz.q: If your results are worse than expected, you should...
options: Report them honestly and explain why
quiz.explain: Honest reporting is the heart of good engineering and research.

lessons.title: Advanced Algorithms
lessons.content:
