What is it? In your first algorithms course you learned how to sort, search and find shortest paths. Advanced Algorithms asks harder questions. What do we do when a problem is so hard that no fast solution is known? What if the data is so huge it doesn't fit in memory? What if a little randomness makes things faster?

Why learn it? Big companies like Google, Uber and Pathao solve problems with millions of inputs every second. A slightly smarter algorithm can save hours of computer time and lots of money. This course also teaches you to prove how good an algorithm is, not just hope it works.

How does it work? You meet NP-hard problems, where even the best known exact methods get painfully slow as the input grows. For these we use approximation algorithms, which promise an answer close to the best, like within 2 times the best. You learn randomized algorithms that flip coins inside the code, network flow for moving things through pipes and roads, amortized analysis for counting the average cost over many steps, and streaming algorithms that read data once and remember only a tiny summary.

Real life example: A Pathao rider has to deliver 15 parcels around Dhaka. Finding the perfect shortest route that visits all 15 is the famous Travelling Salesman Problem, and it is NP-hard. Trying every order would take forever. So the app uses a clever approximation: a route that is maybe a few percent longer than perfect, but found in a second. The rider is happy, and so is the customer.

After this course you can look at a hard problem and decide: should I find the exact answer, a good-enough answer, or a random-but-likely-correct answer? That judgement is what makes a real algorithm designer.
key_points: NP-hard problems have no known fast exact solution.
Approximation algorithms give a guaranteed close-to-best answer quickly.
Randomized and streaming algorithms handle speed and huge data.
You learn to prove how good an algorithm is.
lessons.tip: For every new algorithm, ask two questions: how fast is it, and how close to the best answer is it? Write both on your note card.
lessons.task: Pick 5 places in your area. On paper, try to find the shortest round trip visiting all 5. Count how many different orders exist (hint: it grows very fast) and see why computers need shortcuts.

quiz.q: What does an approximation algorithm do?
options: Always finds the exact best answer
Finds an answer that is provably close to the best, quickly
quiz.explain: Approximation algorithms trade a little accuracy for a lot of speed, with a promise about how far from the best answer they can be.

quiz.q: The Travelling Salesman Problem is an example of...
options: A problem solved instantly by sorting
quiz.explain: Finding the shortest tour through all cities is NP-hard: no known method solves big cases exactly and fast.

quiz.q: Streaming algorithms are useful when...
options: You need a nice user interface
The data is too big to store, so you read it once and keep a small summary
quiz.explain: Streaming algorithms look at each item once and keep only a tiny summary, perfect for huge flows of data.

lessons.title: Advanced Database Systems & Big Data
lessons.content:
What is it? A normal database is like one neat cupboard where a shop keeps its records. But what happens when the data becomes so big that no single cupboard can hold it? This course is about storing and handling giant amounts of data across many computers.

Why learn it? Facebook, Daraz and bKash have billions of records: posts, orders, money transfers. One computer cannot store or process all of that fast enough. Companies need people who know how to spread data across many machines and still keep it correct.

How does it work? First you go deeper into how databases run: query optimization (choosing the fastest way to answer a question) and transactions that keep money transfers safe. Then you meet distributed databases, where data is split into pieces called shards and copied to many machines, called replication. You learn the CAP theorem: when the network breaks, a system must choose between staying consistent and staying available. You also meet NoSQL databases like key-value stores and document stores, and big data tools like MapReduce, Hadoop and Spark that split one huge job into many small jobs running in parallel.

Real life example: Think of the voter list of Bangladesh, with over 10 crore people. If one officer counted everyone alone, it would take years. Instead, every union counts its own people at the same time, then the numbers are added up. That is exactly MapReduce: map means each worker handles its own piece, reduce means adding up the results.

After this course you can design systems that store huge data safely, answer questions fast, and keep working even when some machines fail. Next you can explore data engineering and cloud data platforms.
key_points: Big data is spread across many machines using sharding and replication.
The CAP theorem says you can't have perfect consistency and availability when the network splits.
NoSQL databases trade strict tables for flexibility and scale.
MapReduce and Spark split a huge job into small parallel jobs.
lessons.tip: Don't memorize tools first. Understand the ideas: split the data, copy the data, process in parallel. Every big data tool is built on these.
lessons.task: Take a page of a book. Count the word 'the' alone and time yourself. Then split the page with 2 friends, each counts their part, and add up. That's MapReduce on paper.

quiz.q: What is sharding?
options: Splitting data into pieces stored on different machines
quiz.explain: Sharding splits a big dataset into smaller parts so each machine stores and handles only a piece.

quiz.q: In MapReduce, what does the reduce step do?
options: Combines the partial results from all workers
quiz.explain: Map lets each worker process its own piece; reduce gathers and combines those partial results into the final answer.

quiz.q: The CAP theorem is about the trade-off between...
options: Consistency and availability when the network is partitioned
quiz.explain: CAP says that during a network partition, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability.

lessons.title: Cloud Computing
lessons.content:
What is it? Cloud computing means using someone else's powerful computers over the internet instead of buying your own. It's like using electricity: you don't build a power plant at home, you just plug in and pay for what you use.

Why learn it? Almost every modern app, from Netflix to Chaldal, runs on the cloud, using providers like AWS, Google Cloud or Microsoft Azure. A small startup can launch to millions of users without buying a single server. Cloud skills are among the most wanted in the job market.

How does it work? The key trick is virtualization: one big physical server is split into many virtual machines, each acting like its own computer. Containers like Docker are even lighter boxes that pack an app with everything it needs. Tools like Kubernetes manage thousands of containers. You learn the service models: IaaS (rent raw machines), PaaS (rent a ready platform to run your code) and SaaS (just use the finished software, like Gmail). You also learn auto-scaling, where the system adds more machines when traffic rises and removes them when it drops, and you learn about cost, security and reliability.

Real life example: On Eid sale day, Daraz suddenly gets ten times more visitors. If they had only their own servers, the site would crash. With the cloud, auto-scaling quickly adds more machines for the rush. After Eid, the extra machines are switched off, and Daraz stops paying for them. Like hiring extra cooks only for the wedding day.

After this course you can deploy apps that grow and shrink with demand, choose the right cloud service, and keep costs under control. DevOps and cloud architecture are natural next steps.
key_points: Cloud means renting computing power over the internet, paying for what you use.
Virtualization and containers let one machine act like many.
IaaS, PaaS and SaaS are different levels of what you rent.
Auto-scaling adds or removes machines as traffic changes.
lessons.tip: Most cloud providers have a free tier. Learning by deploying a tiny real app teaches more than reading ten chapters.
lessons.task: List 5 apps on your phone. For each, guess whether it's SaaS for you (you just use it) and whether it likely runs on a cloud like AWS or Google Cloud. Look up one to check.

quiz.q: Gmail is an example of which cloud model for its users?
quiz.explain: With SaaS you just use finished software through the internet. You don't manage any servers or code.

quiz.q: What does virtualization do?
options: Splits one physical machine into many virtual machines
quiz.explain: Virtualization lets one powerful server run many isolated virtual machines, each acting like its own computer.

quiz.q: Auto-scaling helps when...
options: You want to write less code
quiz.explain: Auto-scaling automatically adds machines during traffic spikes and removes them when traffic drops, saving money.

lessons.title: Advanced Computer Networks & Wireless Networks
lessons.content:
What is it? In the first networks course you learned how data travels from one computer to another. This course goes deeper: how the whole internet is routed, how it handles crowds, and how wireless networks like WiFi, 4G and 5G work without any cables.

Why learn it? Video calls, online games and mobile banking all need fast and reliable networks. As more people use phones than computers, wireless networking has become super important. Network engineers keep the whole digital world talking.

How does it work? You study how routers across different companies share paths using BGP, the protocol that glues the internet together. You learn congestion control, where TCP slows down when the road is jammed and speeds up when it's clear. You meet software-defined networking (SDN), where a central program controls many switches. On the wireless side, you learn how radio signals fade and bounce, how many users share the same airwaves, how phones hand over from one cell tower to the next while you move, and how 5G uses higher frequencies and more antennas for more speed.

Real life example: You're on a bus from Dhaka to Chattogram, talking on the phone. Your phone keeps switching from one tower to another along the highway, and the call doesn't drop. That smooth switch is called handover. It's like a relay race where runners pass the baton without stopping.

After this course you can understand and design large networks, fix slow connections, and work on mobile and wireless systems. Next you could look into network security or IoT networks.
key_points: BGP connects the networks of different companies into one internet.
Congestion control stops the network from getting jammed.
SDN lets a central program control network switches.
Wireless networks handle fading signals, shared airwaves and handover.
lessons.tip: Draw diagrams for every protocol: who sends what, to whom, and when. Networks make sense when you can see the arrows.
lessons.task: Walk around your home with your phone's WiFi on. Notice where the signal bars drop. Guess why: walls, distance or interference from other devices.

quiz.q: What is handover in mobile networks?
options: Your connection moving from one cell tower to another as you travel
Giving your phone to a friend
quiz.explain: Handover lets your call or data continue as your phone switches between towers while you move.

quiz.q: What does TCP congestion control do?
options: Slows sending when the network is crowded and speeds up when it's clear
quiz.explain: Congestion control adjusts the sending speed so the network doesn't get overloaded.

quiz.q: In software-defined networking (SDN)...
options: A central program controls how many switches forward traffic
Data is stored in paper files
quiz.explain: SDN separates the control logic from the switches, so one central controller can manage the network.

lessons.title: Parallel & High Performance Computing
lessons.content:
What is it? Parallel computing means doing many parts of a job at the same time, instead of one after another. High Performance Computing, or HPC, is about using huge numbers of processors together, like supercomputers, to solve giant problems.

Why learn it? Single processors stopped getting much faster years ago, so today's speed comes from having more cores working together. Weather forecasting, training AI, simulating medicines and even video games need parallel power. Knowing how to split work well is a superpower.

How does it work? You learn about multi-core CPUs and GPUs, which have thousands of tiny cores perfect for doing the same thing to lots of data. You learn shared memory programming with threads and tools like OpenMP, and message passing with MPI, where separate computers send each other messages. You face tricky problems: race conditions, where two workers change the same data at once; deadlocks, where workers wait for each other forever; and load balancing, keeping every worker equally busy. You also meet Amdahl's law, which says the part of a job that can't be split will limit your total speedup.

Real life example: Think of making pitha for a big family event. One person making 500 pithas takes all day. Ten people working together finish much faster. But if there's only one stove for frying, everyone waits at the stove. That stove is the part that can't be parallelized, and Amdahl's law says it decides how fast you can ever finish.

After this course you can make programs use all the cores of a machine, run jobs on clusters and GPUs, and spot what's slowing things down. Next steps include GPU programming with CUDA and scientific computing.
key_points: Parallel computing does many parts of a job at the same time.
GPUs have thousands of small cores for data-heavy work.
Race conditions and deadlocks are common parallel bugs.
Amdahl's law: the part you can't split limits your speedup.
lessons.tip: Before writing parallel code, ask: which parts are independent? Those are the parts you can split. The rest stays in a line.
lessons.task: Pick a home chore like cleaning a room with siblings. Write which steps can happen at the same time and which must wait. Find the bottleneck.

quiz.q: What is a race condition?
options: Two workers changing the same data at the same time, causing wrong results
quiz.explain: A race condition happens when the result depends on which thread gets there first, often giving wrong data.

quiz.q: Amdahl's law tells us that...
options: More cores always means unlimited speed
The part of a job that can't be parallelized limits the total speedup
quiz.explain: Even with infinite workers, the sequential part of a job still takes the same time, capping the speedup.

quiz.q: MPI is mainly used for...
options: Message passing between separate processes or computers
quiz.explain: MPI (Message Passing Interface) lets separate processes, often on different machines, work together by sending messages.

lessons.title: Data Mining
lessons.content:
What is it? Data mining means digging through huge piles of data to find useful patterns hiding inside. Just like miners dig through rock to find gold, data miners dig through data to find knowledge.

Why learn it? Shops, banks, hospitals and apps collect tons of data every day. Raw data is useless until someone finds the meaning in it. Data mining helps businesses predict what customers want, catch fraud and make smarter decisions.

How does it work? First you clean the data, because real data is messy, with missing and wrong values. Then you use different techniques. Association rules find things that happen together, like items bought together. Classification sorts things into known groups, like spam or not spam, using methods like decision trees. Clustering groups similar things together without any labels, like K-means. Outlier detection finds strange, unusual records. Finally, you check whether the patterns are real and useful, not just luck.

Real life example: A superstore like Shwapno looks at millions of receipts and discovers that people who buy chal and dal often also buy oil. So they place oil nearby and give a combo offer. Banks like bKash use outlier detection: if your account suddenly sends lots of money at 3 AM to a strange number, the system flags it as possible fraud.

After this course you can take a big messy dataset and pull out patterns that help people decide better. Next you can go into machine learning and data science more deeply.
key_points: Data mining finds hidden patterns in large data.
Association rules find things that happen together.
Classification uses labels; clustering groups without labels.
Outlier detection catches unusual records like fraud.
lessons.tip: Always look at the data with your own eyes first. Plot it, count it, find weird values. Half of data mining is cleaning.
lessons.task: Collect 10 of your family's shopping lists or receipts. Find two items that often appear together. You just found an association rule.

quiz.q: Grouping customers by similar behavior without any labels is called...
quiz.explain: Clustering groups similar items together when no predefined labels are given, like K-means.

quiz.q: Finding that people who buy bread often buy butter is an example of...
quiz.explain: Association rules discover items that frequently occur together in transactions.

quiz.q: Which technique helps catch unusual transactions like fraud?
quiz.explain: Outlier detection finds records that look very different from normal behavior, such as fraud.

lessons.title: Research Methodology
lessons.content:
What is it? Research Methodology teaches you how to do proper research: how to ask a good question, find what others already did, test your idea fairly and write it up so others can trust it. In an MSc, this is the course that turns you from a learner into a discoverer.

Why learn it? Your MSc thesis needs real research. Without a method, you might spend months on an idea that was already solved, or make claims that don't hold up. Good research also helps in jobs, where you need to test ideas with evidence instead of guessing.

How does it work? You start with a literature review: reading papers to see what's known and where the gap is. Then you write a clear research question and a hypothesis, an educated guess you can test. You design experiments with baselines (what you compare against), datasets and evaluation metrics like accuracy. You learn the basics of statistics to tell if a result is real or just chance. You also learn academic writing, citing sources properly, avoiding plagiarism and research ethics, like getting permission when your study involves people.

Real life example: Say you think a new rice-disease detection app is better than the old one. Just saying 'mine is better' is not research. You test both apps on the same 1000 leaf photos, compare their accuracy, check that the difference isn't luck, and write it all down so another student can repeat it. Now it's research.

After this course you can plan a thesis, read papers smartly and write your own. You'll know how to prove things, not just believe them.
key_points: Literature review shows what's already known and where the gap is.
A hypothesis is a testable guess.
Fair experiments compare against baselines on the same data.
Cite sources, avoid plagiarism and follow research ethics.
lessons.tip: Keep a research diary. Every day write what you tried, what happened and what you'll try next. Your future self will thank you.
lessons.task: Pick a simple question, like 'Do I study better with music or without?'. Write a hypothesis, how you'd test it fairly for a week, and what you'd measure.

quiz.q: What is a literature review for?
options: Finding what is already known and where the research gap is
quiz.explain: A literature review surveys existing work so you don't repeat it and can find an open problem.

quiz.q: A hypothesis is...
quiz.explain: A hypothesis is a clear prediction that your experiments can support or reject.

quiz.q: Why do we compare against a baseline?
options: To show if our method is really better than an existing one
quiz.explain: A baseline gives a fair point of comparison, showing whether the new method actually improves things.

lessons.title: Deep Learning
lessons.content:
What is it? Deep learning is a kind of machine learning that uses artificial neural networks with many layers. Each layer learns a little more, step by step, from simple patterns to complex ideas. It's loosely inspired by how neurons in the brain connect.

Why learn it? Deep learning powers face unlock on your phone, Google Translate, voice assistants, self-driving research and chatbots. Whenever there's lots of data like pictures, sound or text, deep learning often beats older methods. It's one of the hottest areas in CS right now.

How does it work? A neural network is made of neurons that multiply inputs by weights, add them up and pass the result through an activation function. Training means showing the network many examples, measuring how wrong it is with a loss function, and then using backpropagation and gradient descent to slowly fix the weights. You learn special networks: CNNs for images, RNNs and Transformers for sequences like text, and tricks like dropout to stop overfitting, which is when a model memorizes instead of learning.

Real life example: Think of teaching a small child to recognize a cat. You show many cat pictures and say 'cat'. At first they make mistakes, you correct them, and slowly they get it. The first layers learn edges and lines, middle layers learn ears and whiskers, and the last layers say 'cat'. That's exactly how a deep network learns from lots of photos.

After this course you can build and train neural networks with tools like PyTorch or TensorFlow. Next you can specialize in NLP, computer vision or generative AI.
key_points: Deep learning uses neural networks with many layers.
Training = measure the loss, then fix weights with backpropagation and gradient descent.
CNNs suit images; Transformers suit text and sequences.
Overfitting means memorizing instead of learning.
lessons.tip: Start with a tiny network on a tiny dataset and watch the loss go down. Seeing it learn makes all the math click.
lessons.task: Open your phone gallery and search 'food' or 'car'. Your phone found them using a deep learning model. Notice which ones it got wrong and guess why.

quiz.q: What does backpropagation do?
options: Calculates how each weight should change to reduce the error
quiz.explain: Backpropagation computes gradients that tell each weight which direction to move to reduce the loss.

quiz.q: Which network type is most famous for images?
quiz.explain: CNNs use filters that slide over images, making them great at finding visual patterns.

quiz.q: Overfitting means the model...
options: Memorizes the training data and does badly on new data
quiz.explain: An overfitted model learns the training examples too exactly and fails to generalize to new data.

lessons.title: Natural Language Processing
lessons.content:
What is it? Natural Language Processing, or NLP, is about teaching computers to understand and produce human language, like Bangla and English. Computers love numbers, but we talk in words full of jokes, slang and double meanings. NLP is the bridge.

Why learn it? Google Translate, spell checkers, voice typing, spam filters, chatbots and AI assistants are all NLP. For a language like Bangla, which has fewer tools than English, there's a huge need for NLP engineers and researchers.

How does it work? First, text is broken into small pieces called tokens. Then words are turned into numbers called embeddings, where words with similar meanings sit close together. You learn classic tasks: sentiment analysis (is this review happy or angry?), named entity recognition (finding names of people and places), machine translation and question answering. Modern NLP uses Transformers with attention, which let the model look at every word in a sentence and decide which ones matter most. Large language models are giant Transformers trained on huge amounts of text.

Real life example: You write a Facebook comment in Banglish: 'khub bhalo laglo vai'. An NLP system has to figure out this is Bangla in English letters, and that the feeling is positive. Another example: when you type in Gboard and it suggests the next word, a language model is guessing what you'll say next.

After this course you can build text classifiers, chatbots and translation tools, and maybe help Bangla get better AI tools. Speech processing and large language models are great next steps.
key_points: NLP helps computers understand and generate human language.
Text is split into tokens and turned into number vectors called embeddings.
Common tasks: sentiment, named entities, translation, question answering.
Transformers use attention to focus on the important words.
lessons.tip: Work with a language you know well, like Bangla. You'll spot errors that a non-speaker would miss.
lessons.task: Type a Bangla sentence into Google Translate and translate it to English and back. See what changed. Where did the machine get confused?

quiz.q: What is sentiment analysis?
options: Finding if a text is positive, negative or neutral
quiz.explain: Sentiment analysis detects the emotion or opinion in a piece of text.

quiz.q: What are word embeddings?
options: Numbers that represent words, with similar words close together
quiz.explain: Embeddings turn words into vectors so meaning can be measured as distance.

quiz.q: The attention mechanism in Transformers helps the model...
options: Focus on the most relevant words in a sentence
quiz.explain: Attention lets each word look at all other words and weigh which ones matter most for meaning.

lessons.title: Computer Vision
lessons.content:
What is it? Computer vision is about teaching computers to see and understand pictures and videos. For a computer, a photo is just a big grid of numbers, one for each pixel. Computer vision turns those numbers into meaning: that's a face, that's a bus, that's a cricket ball.

Why learn it? Face unlock, Google Lens, medical scans, self-driving cars, factory quality checks and crop disease detection all use computer vision. Cameras are everywhere, so the need to understand images is everywhere too.

How does it work? You start with image basics: pixels, color channels and filters that find edges. Then you learn the main tasks. Image classification says what's in the picture. Object detection draws boxes around each object, using models like YOLO. Segmentation colors every pixel by what it belongs to. You also learn tracking objects across video frames and 3D vision, like estimating depth from two cameras, just as our two eyes do. Most modern methods use deep learning, especially CNNs and vision Transformers.

Real life example: Think of Dhaka traffic cameras. A computer vision system can count how many buses, cars and rickshaws pass each minute, spot a vehicle breaking the signal, and read its number plate. Or a farmer takes a photo of a rice leaf, and an app tells if it has blast disease.

After this course you can build apps that recognize, detect and track things in images and video. Next steps include robotics, medical imaging and augmented reality.
key_points: To a computer, an image is a grid of pixel numbers.
Classification says what; detection says where with boxes.
Segmentation labels every single pixel.
Modern vision mostly uses CNNs and vision Transformers.
lessons.tip: Always visualize your model's outputs on real images. Boxes in the wrong place teach you more than any accuracy number.
lessons.task: Use Google Lens on 5 objects around you. Note which ones it recognizes correctly and which it fails on. Think about lighting and angle.

quiz.q: For a computer, an image is basically...
options: A grid of numbers representing pixels
quiz.explain: Every image is stored as numbers for each pixel's brightness or color.

quiz.q: Which task draws boxes around each object in a picture?
quiz.explain: Object detection finds where objects are and draws bounding boxes around them, like YOLO does.

quiz.q: Segmentation means...
options: Labeling every pixel with what it belongs to
quiz.explain: Segmentation classifies each pixel, so you get the exact shape of every object.

lessons.title: Reinforcement Learning
lessons.content:
What is it? Reinforcement learning, or RL, is learning by trial and error. An agent tries actions in an environment, gets rewards for good moves and penalties for bad ones, and slowly figures out the best way to behave. Nobody gives it the right answers; it learns from experience.

Why learn it? RL taught computers to beat world champions at Go and play video games better than humans. It's used in robotics, recommending content, controlling traffic lights, managing power in data centers and fine-tuning chatbots with human feedback.

How does it work? The key parts are the agent, the environment, states (the current situation), actions and rewards. The agent learns a policy, which is a rule for which action to take in each state. A value function estimates how much total future reward a state is worth. You learn the exploration vs exploitation balance: try new things to learn more, or use what already works? Classic methods include Q-learning, and deep RL combines this with neural networks, like Deep Q-Networks.

Real life example: Think of learning to ride a bicycle. Nobody can give you an exact formula. You try, you wobble, you fall, which is a penalty. You balance a bit longer, which feels great, a reward. After many tries, your brain learns the policy. Or think of training a pet: give it a treat when it sits, and soon it sits on command.

After this course you can build agents that learn to make decisions over time. Next you can explore robotics, game AI and multi-agent systems.
key_points: RL learns by trial and error using rewards and penalties.
The agent learns a policy: which action to take in each state.
Balance exploration (try new) and exploitation (use what works).
Q-learning and Deep Q-Networks are classic methods.
lessons.tip: Start with tiny grid-world problems you can draw on paper. Once you can follow the agent by hand, bigger problems feel natural.
lessons.task: Think of a game you got better at, like Ludo or a phone game. Write down what the 'rewards' and 'penalties' were and how your strategy changed over time.

quiz.q: In reinforcement learning, the agent learns mainly from...
options: A teacher giving the correct answer each time
Rewards and penalties from its actions
quiz.explain: RL agents improve by trying actions and getting reward signals, not labelled correct answers.

quiz.q: What is a policy in RL?
options: A rule for which action to take in each state
quiz.explain: A policy maps each situation (state) to an action. Learning a good policy is the goal of RL.

quiz.q: The exploration vs exploitation trade-off is about...
options: Trying new actions vs using the best known action
quiz.explain: The agent must balance learning more by exploring and earning reward by exploiting what it already knows.

lessons.title: Robotics
lessons.content:
What is it? Robotics is about building machines that can sense the world, think about it and act on it. A robot mixes everything: mechanical parts, electronics, sensors and software. In CS, the focus is mostly on the brain: how a robot knows where it is and decides what to do.

Why learn it? Robots work in factories, warehouses, hospitals and farms, and even clean our floors. Drones deliver medicine and map land. Robotics is where AI leaves the screen and moves in the real world, which makes it super exciting and super tricky.

How does it work? Every robot runs a loop: sense, think, act. Sensors like cameras, LiDAR and encoders read the world. Kinematics is the math of how robot arms and wheels move. Localization figures out where the robot is, and SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) lets it build a map while finding itself in it. Path planning finds a safe way to the goal, using algorithms like A*. Control, like PID controllers, keeps movement smooth and accurate. Tools like ROS (Robot Operating System) help put it all together.

Real life example: A robot vacuum cleaner in a flat. When it starts, it doesn't know the room. It bumps around, uses sensors to map walls and furniture, remembers where it has cleaned and plans a path to the dirty spots. Then it goes back to its charger by itself. That's sense, think, act, all in one little round robot.

After this course you can program robots to move, map and plan. Next you can dive into autonomous vehicles, drones or robot learning with RL.
key_points: Robots run a sense, think, act loop.
SLAM builds a map while locating the robot in it.
Path planning (like A*) finds a safe route to the goal.
PID control keeps motion smooth and accurate.
lessons.tip: Real sensors are noisy. Always test in the real world early, because what works in simulation often surprises you outside it.
lessons.task: Blindfold yourself (safely!) and try to walk from your bed to the door by counting steps. Notice how small errors add up. Robots face the same problem, and that's why localization matters.

quiz.q: What is the basic loop every robot runs?
quiz.explain: Robots sense the world, decide what to do and then act, again and again.

quiz.q: SLAM stands for...
quiz.explain: SLAM lets a robot build a map of an unknown place while figuring out where it is inside that map.

quiz.q: A PID controller is used to...
options: Keep a robot's movement smooth and on target
quiz.explain: PID control constantly corrects errors so motors reach and hold the desired position or speed.

levels.title: MSc: The future and your thesis

lessons.title: Internet of Things (IoT)
lessons.content:
Imagine if your fan, your water tank and even your rice cooker could talk to the internet. That's the Internet of Things, or IoT. It's all about everyday objects that have tiny computers, sensors and a network connection inside them, so they can collect data and do things on their own or when you tell them from your phone.

Why learn it? Because billions of these little devices are already around us: smart watches, smart meters, traffic cameras, farm sensors, even prepaid electricity meters. Someone has to design them, connect them safely and make sense of the mountain of data they send. That someone could be you.

Here's how it works. First, sensors measure something, like temperature, light, motion or soil moisture. A small chip called a microcontroller (think Arduino or ESP32) reads that value. Then it sends the data over a network like Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, LoRa or mobile data, often using light protocols such as MQTT. The data goes to a server or the cloud, where it's stored and analyzed. Finally, actuators do something back in the real world, like turning on a motor or a light. In the MSc course you also study edge computing (doing the thinking close to the device), saving battery power, and keeping all these devices secure, because a hacked camera is a real problem.

Real life example: a farmer in Rajshahi puts a soil moisture sensor in the field. When the soil gets too dry, the sensor tells a small controller, which switches on the water pump and sends a message to the farmer's phone: pump on. No need to walk to the field at noon in the heat. The same idea runs smart water tanks in Dhaka flats that stop the pump before the tank overflows.

After this course you'll be able to plan an IoT system from sensor to cloud to app, pick the right network and protocol, and think about power and security. Next, look at embedded systems, cloud computing and data analytics, since IoT sits right where they meet.
key_points: IoT means everyday objects with sensors, small chips and a network connection.
The flow is: sensor reads, microcontroller processes, network sends, cloud stores, actuator acts.
Light protocols like MQTT and networks like Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and LoRa connect devices.
Power saving, edge computing and security are the big challenges.
lessons.tip: IoT clicks fastest when you build something tiny. A cheap ESP32 board and one sensor will teach you more than ten slides.
lessons.task: Walk around your home and list 5 things that could become IoT devices. For each one, write what sensor it needs, what data it would send, and what action it could take.

quiz.q: What does an IoT device usually need?
options: Only a big screen and a keyboard
A sensor or actuator, a small chip and a network connection
A full desktop computer inside it
quiz.explain: An IoT device senses or acts on the world, has a small processor like a microcontroller, and connects to a network to share data.

quiz.q: What is MQTT commonly used for in IoT?
options: Sending small messages between devices and servers in a lightweight way
quiz.explain: MQTT is a light publish and subscribe messaging protocol, great for small devices with weak networks and little power.

quiz.q: What does edge computing mean?
options: Processing data close to the device instead of sending everything to a far away cloud
Putting computers on the edge of a table
Only using the cloud for everything
quiz.explain: Edge computing does some of the thinking near the device, which cuts delay, saves bandwidth and can keep data more private.

lessons.title: Blockchain
lessons.content:
Picture a notebook that the whole class keeps together. Every time someone gives someone else a pencil, it's written in the notebook, and everyone has their own copy. Nobody can secretly erase a line, because all the other copies would disagree. That's basically a blockchain: a shared record book, copied across many computers, where old entries can't be quietly changed.

Why learn it? Blockchain lets people who don't fully trust each other agree on one true record without a middle boss like a bank. It powers cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, but also ideas like tracking where goods come from, digital certificates and smart contracts. Knowing it also helps you tell real uses apart from hype.

Here's how it works. Data is packed into blocks. Each block holds a cryptographic hash of the block before it, a short fingerprint. Change even one letter in an old block and its fingerprint changes, which breaks the chain after it, so cheating is easy to spot. Many computers, called nodes, keep copies. To add a new block they follow a consensus rule: Proof of Work makes them solve a hard puzzle, Proof of Stake picks validators based on coins they lock up. Digital signatures prove who sent what. Smart contracts are small programs stored on the chain that run automatically, like a vending machine: put money in, get the item out, no shopkeeper needed. In the MSc course you also study scalability limits, energy cost, privacy and attacks like the 51 percent attack.

Real life example: think of a garments supply chain. Cotton comes from a farm, goes to a mill, then a factory in Gazipur, then a ship, then a shop abroad. If every step is recorded on a shared blockchain, a buyer can check the whole journey and nobody can quietly fake a step later. Another example: a university could put degree certificates on a chain, so an employer can verify them in seconds.

After this course you'll understand hashing, consensus and smart contracts, and you'll be able to judge when a blockchain truly helps and when a normal database is simpler and better. Next, dig into cryptography and distributed systems.
key_points: A blockchain is a shared, copied ledger where old records are very hard to change.
Each block stores the hash of the previous block, linking them into a chain.
Consensus methods like Proof of Work and Proof of Stake decide who adds the next block.
Smart contracts are programs on the chain that run automatically when conditions are met.
lessons.tip: Always ask: do we really need a blockchain here, or would a normal database do? Being able to answer that makes you sound like a real expert.
lessons.task: On paper, make 4 blocks. In each, write a small transaction and a made-up fingerprint built from the previous block's fingerprint plus its own text. Now change block 2 and see how blocks 3 and 4 no longer match.

quiz.q: Why is it hard to secretly change an old block?
options: Because blocks are written in pen
Because blocks are deleted after one day
Because each block holds the previous block's hash, so changing one breaks the chain and the other copies disagree
quiz.explain: Hashes link the blocks. A change alters the fingerprint, breaks every link after it, and doesn't match the copies held by other nodes.

quiz.q: What is a smart contract?
options: A paper contract signed by a lawyer
A program stored on the blockchain that runs automatically when its conditions are met
quiz.explain: Smart contracts are code on the chain. Like a vending machine, they act automatically once the rules are satisfied.

quiz.q: What does a consensus mechanism do?
options: Helps all nodes agree on which block gets added next
Chooses the color of the coin
quiz.explain: Consensus rules like Proof of Work or Proof of Stake let many independent computers agree on one shared history.

lessons.title: Quantum Computing
lessons.content:
A normal computer thinks in bits, and a bit is either 0 or 1, like a light switch that's either off or on. A quantum computer uses qubits. A qubit can be in a mix of 0 and 1 at the same time until you look at it, a bit like a spinning coin that isn't heads or tails yet. Quantum computing is about using these strange rules of tiny particles to solve certain problems in a totally new way.

Why learn it? For some special problems, quantum computers could be hugely faster: simulating molecules for new medicines, some optimization problems, and breaking some of today's encryption. That last one is why the world is already moving to post-quantum cryptography. It's still an early field, so people who understand it now will be in demand later.

Here's how it works. Superposition lets a qubit hold a mix of 0 and 1. Entanglement links qubits so that measuring one tells you something about the other, no matter how far apart. Quantum gates, like the Hadamard gate or CNOT, change qubit states, and a list of gates forms a quantum circuit. When you finally measure, the qubit collapses to plain 0 or 1, with certain probabilities. The trick of a quantum algorithm is to use interference, making wrong answers cancel out and right answers grow stronger. Famous algorithms: Shor's algorithm can factor big numbers fast, which threatens RSA, and Grover's algorithm searches an unsorted list in about the square root of the steps. Real machines today are noisy and small, so error correction is a huge research topic.

Real life example: imagine finding one friend's phone number in a messy, unsorted list of a million numbers. A normal computer may check up to a million entries. Grover's algorithm needs only about a thousand quantum steps. Another example: designing a new medicine means understanding how molecules behave, and molecules follow quantum rules, so a quantum computer is a natural fit to simulate them.

After this course you'll be able to read and draw simple quantum circuits, explain superposition and entanglement, and know which problems quantum computers help with and which they don't. Next, try a free simulator like IBM Quantum or Qiskit and brush up your linear algebra, because qubits are really just vectors.
key_points: Qubits can be in a superposition of 0 and 1 until they are measured.
Entanglement links qubits so their results are connected.
Quantum gates build circuits; measurement gives 0 or 1 with some probability.
Shor's algorithm threatens RSA, Grover's speeds up search, but today's machines are small and noisy.
lessons.tip: Don't fight the weirdness with everyday intuition. Treat qubits as vectors and gates as matrices, and the math will guide you.
lessons.task: Flip a coin 20 times and write down the results. Think of the coin in the air as a superposition and the landed coin as a measurement. Then write 3 lines on why you only ever see heads or tails, never both.

quiz.q: What makes a qubit different from a normal bit?
options: It can only store the number 2
It can be in a superposition of 0 and 1 until measured
quiz.explain: A classical bit is 0 or 1. A qubit can hold a mix of both until measurement makes it pick one.

quiz.q: Why does quantum computing worry security experts?
options: Shor's algorithm could break RSA style encryption on a big enough quantum computer
quiz.explain: Shor's algorithm factors big numbers efficiently, which would break RSA. That's why post-quantum cryptography is being adopted.

quiz.q: What is a big problem with quantum computers today?
options: They are noisy and small, so errors are a major challenge
They cannot be programmed at all
quiz.explain: Current machines have few, error-prone qubits. Quantum error correction is a key research area.

lessons.title: Bioinformatics
lessons.content:
Every living thing carries an instruction book inside its cells called DNA. That book is written with just four letters: A, C, G and T. A human's book has about 3 billion letters! Bioinformatics is where computer science meets biology: using programs and algorithms to read, compare and understand these huge biological texts.

Why learn it? Because biology turned into a data problem. Labs can now read DNA fast and cheap, and they produce mountains of data that no human could ever go through by hand. Bioinformatics helps find disease genes, track viruses during pandemics, design medicines and improve crops. It's one of the most meaningful places to use your coding skills.

Here's how it works. First, sequencing machines read DNA in tiny pieces, and algorithms stitch them back together, like rebuilding a torn newspaper; this is called genome assembly. Then sequence alignment compares two sequences to see how similar they are, using dynamic programming algorithms like Needleman-Wunsch and Smith-Waterman, or fast tools like BLAST for searching huge databases. Phylogenetic trees show how species or virus strains are related, like a family tree. Other topics include predicting protein structures, finding which genes are switched on, and using machine learning on biological data. Behind it all are the CS basics you know: strings, graphs, hashing, dynamic programming and probability.

Real life example: during COVID-19, scientists in Bangladesh and around the world sequenced the virus from patients. By aligning those sequences and building family trees, they could see which variant was spreading, like Delta or Omicron, and how it arrived. Another example: rice scientists compare the DNA of rice varieties to find genes that help rice survive floods or salty water, which matters a lot for coastal areas.

After this course you'll be able to work with DNA and protein sequences, run alignments, use public databases and tools, and connect biology questions to algorithms. Next, look at machine learning for biology, and learn Python with Biopython to start playing with real sequences.
key_points: Bioinformatics uses computing to analyze biological data like DNA and proteins.
DNA is a long string of A, C, G and T, so string algorithms matter a lot.
Sequence alignment, often with dynamic programming or BLAST, measures similarity.
Uses include tracking viruses, finding disease genes and improving crops.
lessons.tip: You don't need to be a biology expert to start. Treat DNA as text and learn the biology bit by bit as each problem needs it.
lessons.task: Write two short DNA strings, like ACGTTGCA and ACGATGCA. Line them up and count how many positions match. That match count is a very simple alignment score.

quiz.q: Which four letters make up DNA?
quiz.explain: DNA is built from four bases: adenine, cytosine, guanine and thymine, written A, C, G and T.

quiz.q: What does sequence alignment do?
options: Lines up two biological sequences to measure how similar they are
quiz.explain: Alignment lines up sequences, allowing matches, mismatches and gaps, to find similarity and shared ancestry.

quiz.q: How did bioinformatics help during COVID-19?
options: It compared virus sequences to track which variants were spreading
quiz.explain: Sequencing and comparing virus genomes let scientists identify variants like Delta and Omicron and follow how they spread.

lessons.title: Advanced Cyber Security
lessons.content:
In BSc you learned the basics of keeping computers safe. Advanced cyber security is the next level: thinking like a real attacker, defending big systems, and handling attacks when they actually happen. Think of it as moving from locking your own door to protecting a whole bank, with guards, cameras, alarms and a plan for when someone still breaks in.

Why learn it? Because everything we care about runs on computers now: mobile banking, hospital records, power grids, elections. Attacks keep getting smarter, and there's a big shortage of skilled security people around the world, including in Bangladesh where digital services like bKash and online banking keep growing.

Here's how it works. You start with threat modeling: what are we protecting, who might attack, and how? Then you study advanced attacks: web attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting, malware and ransomware, phishing and social engineering, and attacks on networks and the cloud. On the defense side you learn about defense in depth, which means many layers of protection, zero trust, which means never trust any user or device automatically, intrusion detection systems, and secure coding. Penetration testing means attacking your own system, with permission, to find holes first. Digital forensics is detective work after an attack, and incident response is the step-by-step plan for when things go wrong. Research topics include using machine learning to spot attacks and preparing for post-quantum cryptography.

Real life example: someone gets an SMS saying their mobile wallet is blocked and asking for the PIN and OTP. That's phishing plus social engineering, and it targets the human, not the computer. A good defense is layered: the app never asks for the PIN by SMS, the system flags weird logins from a new phone, there's a limit on how much money can move, and customers are taught never to share the OTP. If one layer fails, the next one catches it.

After this course you'll be able to model threats, find and fix common weaknesses, design layered defenses and respond calmly to an incident. Next, practice legally on capture the flag challenges and platforms like TryHackMe or Hack The Box, and always hack only what you have permission to test.
key_points: Threat modeling asks what to protect, from whom, and how they might attack.
Defense in depth and zero trust use many layers and trust nothing by default.
Penetration testing is authorized attacking to find weaknesses first.
Forensics and incident response handle what happens during and after an attack.
lessons.tip: Learn to think like an attacker, but act like a guardian. Always get written permission before testing any system.
lessons.task: Pick an app you use every day. Write down 3 ways someone might try to break into your account and one layer of defense for each, like a strong password, two factor login or not sharing an OTP.

quiz.q: What does zero trust mean?
options: Trust everyone inside the office network
Never trust any user or device automatically, always verify
quiz.explain: Zero trust assumes no user or device is safe by default, so every access request must be checked.

quiz.q: What is penetration testing?
options: Testing how strong a pen is
Breaking into any system you like
Attacking a system with permission to find its weaknesses before real attackers do
quiz.explain: Pen testing is ethical, authorized hacking whose goal is to discover and fix holes.

quiz.q: An SMS asking for your wallet PIN and OTP is an example of...
quiz.explain: It tricks a person into giving away secrets. Real services never ask for your PIN or OTP like that.

lessons.title: MSc Thesis
lessons.content:
Your MSc thesis is your own little adventure into the unknown. In normal courses, a teacher gives you questions that already have answers. In a thesis, you pick a question that nobody has fully answered yet, try to answer it carefully, and write it all up so others can learn from it. It's like being a detective and a writer at the same time.

Why do it? Because it teaches you to think on your own, which is the real goal of a master's degree. You learn to read research papers, design experiments, handle failure and explain your work clearly. A good thesis can turn into a published paper, helps a lot with PhD applications and scholarships abroad, and shows employers you can solve hard, open problems.

Here's how it works. First, find a topic you actually find interesting, and talk with your supervisor. Then do a literature review: read what others have done so you know where the gap is. Turn that gap into a clear research question. Next, pick a method: build a system, run experiments, collect data or prove something. Do the work, test it fairly against existing methods using proper metrics, and keep notes and code organized with tools like Git. Finally, write the thesis, usually with introduction, related work, method, results, discussion and conclusion, and defend it in front of a committee. Honesty matters most: report what really happened, cite every source, and never copy.

Real life example: say you notice that Bangla text on social media is full of spelling mixes and Banglish, and most sentiment analysis tools fail on it. Your question could be: can a model trained on mixed Bangla and Banglish text detect sentiment better? You'd collect and label data, try a few models, compare them with existing ones, and write up what worked and what didn't. Even a small improvement, clearly shown, is a real contribution.

After your thesis you'll know how to do research from start to finish: find a gap, plan, test, write and defend. Keep it going by submitting your work to a conference or journal, and treat your supervisor's feedback as a gift, not a punishment.
key_points: A thesis answers an open question with careful, original work.
Steps: topic, literature review, research question, method, experiments, writing, defense.
Compare your results fairly with existing methods using clear metrics.
Honesty, citing sources and organized code and notes are non negotiable.
lessons.tip: Start small and specific. A sharp question you can actually finish beats a giant question you can only start.
lessons.task: Write down 3 problems you've noticed around you that technology could help with. For each, turn it into a one line research question that starts with: Can we... or How well does...

quiz.q: What is a literature review for?
options: Learning what others have already done so you can find the gap your work fills
quiz.explain: Reviewing existing research shows what's known and where the open question is, so your work adds something new.

quiz.q: Which is the better thesis question?
options: Can a model trained on mixed Bangla and Banglish text detect sentiment better than existing tools?
How do we solve all of AI?
quiz.explain: A good research question is specific, testable and doable in the time you have.

quiz.q: What must you always do in a thesis?
options: Copy text from papers without citing
Report results honestly and cite every source you use
quiz.explain: Research integrity is the foundation. Honest results and proper citations keep your work trustworthy.
